items.x: In May 2026 Trump postponed signing a draft order that gave government 90 days of pre-launch access, saying it 'could have been a blocker'; Zuckerberg, Musk and David Sacks reportedly spoke with him first. The June 2026 order (EO 14409) instead set up a voluntary framework with up to 30 days of access.

items.p: According to the pacing.tech authors, why can dangerous-capability evaluations 'generally only set a lower bound' on what a model can do?
items.answer: Because of elicitation challenges (testers may not find the right way to draw out a capability) and because models may alter their behavior when they recognize they are being evaluated. They add that evaluation results often correspond poorly to real-world behavior.
keys: Elicitation may fall short
Models may behave differently when they recognize evaluation
Weak link to real-world behavior
items.x: Related items in the pacing.tech appendix longlist include an elicitation budget per dangerous-capability evaluation and a sandbagging detection protocol.

items.p: Match each intervention listed in the pacing.tech appendix to a description of it.
pairs: Elicitation budget per dangerous-capability eval
Minimum effort testers must spend drawing out a capability (cites METR's elicitation protocol)
Sandbagging detection protocol
Checks for models strategically underperforming on evaluations (cites van der Weij et al. 2024)
Third-party evaluator access depth
How far outside evaluators can see beyond black-box queries (cites Casper et al. 2024)
Pre-deployment testing window with government access
Time for government to test a model before release (cites the June 2026 order and FRONTIER Act)
items.x: The appendix gives no specific budget level or detection method for these items, and its authors say listing a lever is not an argument for using it.

items.p: What does the 2024 paper 'Black-Box Access is Insufficient for Rigorous AI Audits' (Casper et al.) argue?
items.answer: That auditors who can only query a model's inputs and outputs cannot audit it rigorously; they need deeper access, such as to model internals (weights and activations) and information about how the model was trained and deployed.
keys: Black-box query access is not enough
Need access to internals such as weights
Need training and deployment information
items.x: The pacing.tech appendix cites it for its 'third-party evaluator access depth' item. The pacing.tech authors also describe a general tradeoff: more accurate oversight usually requires more access to information that might otherwise be private.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors describe a three-way tradeoff that any pacing or verification intervention faces. What are the three elements?
items.answer: False positives (acting when there is no real danger), false negatives (missing real danger), and intrusiveness (how much oversight and private information the intervention requires). More accuracy usually means closer scrutiny and more access to private information.
keys: False positives
False negatives
Intrusiveness or oversight burden
items.x: They note indirect tools such as taxes, buyouts and liability need no surveillance to operate, and they list technical routes to high assurance with minimal invasiveness (such as LLM-based oversight and cryptographic guarantees) as a research priority.

items.p: Risk: a lab releases a model with dangerous capabilities that its own internal tests missed or underestimated. Name two policies proposed to catch this.
items.answer: Examples: government pre-deployment testing; mandatory third-party audits or independent evaluations; embedded evaluators inside labs; minimum elicitation budgets and sandbagging detection protocols; deeper evaluator access to model internals; mandatory disclosure of dangerous-capability results.
keys: Government pre-deployment testing
Third-party audits or evaluations
Embedded evaluators
Elicitation budgets or sandbagging checks
Deeper evaluator access
items.x: Supporters of outside testing argue that in-house evaluation misses flaws outsiders find (Longpre et al.).

items.p: What is an 'independent verification organization' (IVO) system for AI, such as the one California created with SB 813 (signed Sept 2026)?
items.answer: The state designates or certifies private organizations (IVOs), independent of the companies they check, to assess AI models and systems against state requirements. Government sets the application rules and criteria and can suspend or terminate an IVO. Developers are not compelled to use one; proposals in this family often reward participation with a legal benefit.
keys: State certifies private verifiers
Verifiers must be independent of those assessed
Government can suspend or revoke them
Participation voluntary for developers
items.x: Under SB 813, California's Government Operations Agency must certify the first IVOs by January 1, 2028. As of Oct 2026, Connecticut has enacted a voluntary pilot and Ohio has a bill. The federal FRONTIER Act would instead require the very largest developers to retain a federally licensed IVO.

items.p: How do supporters of 'regulatory markets' (certified private AI verifiers) say the approach would work better than direct rules?
items.answer: Legislators and agencies lack technical staff and speed to write detailed rules for fast-changing AI. A regulated market of private verifiers could build expertise, pay competitive salaries and update methods faster, while government oversight of the verifiers keeps them honest, and a liability benefit draws developers in without a mandate.
keys: Government lacks staff and speed
Private verifiers build expertise and pay more
Methods update faster
Government oversees the verifiers
Liability benefit draws developers in
items.x: The idea is most associated with Gillian Hadfield and Jack Clark ('Regulatory Markets: The Future of AI Governance').

items.p: Under a regulatory-markets design, government certifies private verifiers that developers choose and pay, often for liability protection. What objections do critics raise? Give one or two.
items.answer: Examples: when developers pick and pay verifiers, competition pushes verifiers toward leniency (Gabriel Weil); the accredited-auditor ecosystem does not exist yet (NetChoice); government needs its own examination capacity to judge verifiers (ARI); the FRONTIER Act's preemption would apply at once while the verifier market takes years (ARI's Brad Carson).
keys: Race to leniency (Weil)
Ecosystem does not exist yet (NetChoice)
Government needs its own capacity to judge verifiers (ARI)
Oversight gap under FRONTIER preemption (ARI)
items.x: Weil's proposed fix is mandatory liability insurance so verifiers or insurers bear the cost of misses. ARI's fix is a hybrid where government examines developers itself and keeps the final judgment.

items.p: Match each law or proposal to its design for private AI verifiers.
pairs: California SB 813
State-certified verifiers that developers choose to use
FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925)
Mandatory federally licensed verifier for the largest developers
ARI blueprint (Americans for Responsible Innovation)
Government examiners keep final judgment and accredit verifiers
California AB 1405
Registry of AI auditors with independence rules
items.x: These range from a light registry to a mandate. Critics note voluntary versions bind no one who declines.

items.p: New York's RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315 require large frontier developers to file disclosure statements before operating in the state. How does this 'registration' differ from licensing?
o: Registration means filing basic information, with no government approval needed; licensing makes building or releasing models conditional on revocable government permission.
Registration requires a government safety test before every release; licensing only requires a fee.
Registration applies to individual engineers; licensing applies to companies.
Registration is enforced by federal agencies; licensing only by states.
ow: Registration involves no safety test or approval; licensing is the version with approval.
Professional licensing of engineers is a separate proposal (Chinmayi Sharma); state registration covers companies.
Both state registration laws are enforced by the states.
items.x: Registration aims at knowing who the frontier developers are so other rules can reach them. As of Oct 2026, approval-based licensing appears in the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (Sanders, Casar), and the June 2026 executive order disclaims mandatory licensing.

items.p: Proposals would require frontier AI developers to obtain a government license or charter before training or deploying top models. What objections have critics raised? Give one or two.
items.answer: Examples: FDA-style approval fits frontier AI poorly because the product is hard to define and harms are deeply uncertain (Daniel Carpenter and Carson Ezell, Harvard); the Hawley-Blumenthal bill barring deployment until developers join an Energy Department program is an executive power grab (Cato); the Trump administration's June 2026 order rejects mandatory licensing or preclearance.
keys: Product hard to define, harms uncertain (Carpenter and Ezell)
Executive power grab (Cato Institute)
Administration disclaims licensing (June 2026 order)
items.x: Supporters argue disclosure and liability act after the fact, while a license lets government stop a dangerous model before it ships and gives leverage over a few high-value companies.

items.p: Match each proposed or existing frontier AI regulator to its source.
pairs: Cabinet-level Department of AI
Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (Sanders, Casar)
Safety board inside the Commerce Department
AI Safety Board Act (Warner)
Commerce Under Secretary for AI Security
FRONTIER Act (Obernolte, Trahan)
Office inside a state financial regulator, funded by fees
New York's RAISE Act (Department of Financial Services)
items.x: Supporters of a dedicated regulator argue US oversight is split across voluntary CAISI testing, state attorneys general and agencies with no AI mandate, so nobody has both expertise and authority. The EU AI Office has enforced general-purpose model rules since August 2026.

items.p: Proposals would create a dedicated federal regulator for frontier AI. What objections or weaknesses have critics pointed to? Give one or two.
items.answer: Examples: Sen. Ted Cruz blocked the AI Safety Board Act, saying it gives Commerce too much authority and that Congress should not legislate hastily; Dan Parshall (Canary Institute) says the FRONTIER Act's Under Secretary lacks Senate confirmation, subpoena power and funding, so it may exist only on paper; IFP says even the existing testing body, CAISI, is underfunded.
keys: Too much agency discretion (Cruz)
Paper regulator without powers or funding (Parshall)
Existing capacity underfunded (IFP)
items.x: The pacing.tech authors list 'regulator capacity' as an intervention and note that the US government AI evaluator's nominal annual budget is less than some individual frontier researchers' salaries.

items.p: What does IFP (Institute for Progress) recommend Congress do for CAISI, the US government's AI testing center, in its 2026 report on automated AI research?
items.answer: Fund it with at least 84 million dollars a year, give it a direct line to a senior White House or cabinet-level official, and let it place staff inside frontier companies, organize third-party evaluators, and contract directly with companies.
keys: At least 84 million dollars a year
Direct line to senior officials
Staff placed inside frontier companies
Organize third-party evaluators
items.x: IFP calls 84 million dollars a minimum bar. An earlier IFP analysis (May 2026) put CAISI's funding at about 15 million dollars as of fiscal year 2026.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors say 'control surfaces earlier in the chain are easier to observe and constrain'. What do they mean, and what is the tradeoff?
items.answer: Control surfaces are the points where an intervention can act (such as chips, compute, model weights, or access). Early inputs like compute are physical and trackable, so an overseer can be much more certain where chips are; copied model weights cannot be verified as fully accounted for. The tradeoff is that early surfaces are less precisely targeted at the actual hazard.
keys: Control surfaces: points where interventions act
Compute is physical and trackable
Copied weights cannot be fully accounted for
Earlier surfaces are less precisely targeted
items.x: The authors add that coordination lasts longer when compliance can be checked without relying on participants' goodwill, which favors measurable thresholds over holistic judgments.

units.title: Liability and lab governance
units.desc: Lawsuits, insurance, safe harbors, whistleblowers, antitrust carve-outs and lab boards: tools that change what AI developers are legally and financially accountable for.

items.p: A statutory duty of care would require frontier AI developers to take reasonable care to avoid causing or enabling catastrophic harm, enforced through lawsuits or attorney general actions. What failure do supporters say it targets?
items.answer: Labs under competitive pressure skipping safety work whose costs fall on the lab while the benefits are spread across society. A legal duty turns those skipped precautions into legal exposure, so lawyers and boards treat testing, security and mitigation as mandatory.
keys: Competitive pressure leads labs to skip safety work
Duty turns skipped precautions into legal exposure
items.x: Supporters also like that a negligence standard is flexible: courts can judge new harm pathways (internal deployment, weight theft, open release) without Congress listing each one. California's SB 1047 (vetoed 2024) used this structure.

items.p: Proposal: a law requiring frontier AI developers to take 'reasonable care' to prevent catastrophic harms, enforceable in court. Name one or two objections critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: Gabriel Weil argues negligence is too weak for catastrophic AI risk and favors strict liability, treating frontier AI as an abnormally dangerous activity; Ketan Ramakrishnan argues the threat of tort liability can discourage developers from investigating and disclosing risks; liability arrives too late, and exceeds any firm's assets, for a true catastrophe.
keys: Weil: negligence too weak; prefers strict liability
Ramakrishnan: liability discourages investigating and disclosing risks
Liability comes too late or is unpayable for a real catastrophe
items.x: Ramakrishnan concludes that liability needs a robust regime of ex ante (before-the-fact) regulation alongside it. The 'too late' point is a common critique with no single named author. On the federal Cruz-Klobuchar-Thune draft (reported Sept. 2026), Sen. Cantwell objected to its reliance on company self-testing.

items.p: Which California bill required frontier developers to take 'reasonable care' to avoid critical harms, and what happened to it?
o: SB 1047, which passed the legislature in 2024 and was vetoed by Gov. Newsom in September 2024
SB 53, which was vetoed in 2025
SB 813, which was vetoed in 2026
AB 1405, which was struck down in court in 2025
ow: SB 53 is California's frontier transparency law; it was signed, and it centers on published safety frameworks and incident reporting.
SB 813 was signed in September 2026; it sets up a framework for independent verification organizations that assess AI systems.
AB 1405 was signed in September 2026; it creates a state registry for AI auditors, not a duty of care.
items.x: As of Oct. 2026 no US jurisdiction has enacted a frontier-specific duty of care. A federal Senate draft (Cruz-Klobuchar-Thune) reportedly included one, but talks stalled on Sept. 29, 2026.

items.p: In AI liability debates, what is the key difference between a negligence standard and strict liability for developers?
items.answer: Under negligence, a developer pays only if it failed to take reasonable care. Under strict liability, it pays for harm its system causes even if it took every known precaution, which supporters say gives it a reason to slow down or invent new safeguards when risks are poorly understood.
keys: Negligence: liable only for failing to take reasonable care
Strict: liable regardless of precautions taken
Supporters: strict liability pushes caution when risks are poorly understood
items.x: Gabriel Weil is the leading advocate of strict liability for advanced AI, treating training and deploying frontier systems as an 'abnormally dangerous activity.'

items.p: Gabriel Weil proposes adding punitive damages to AI liability cases. What problem does he say this solves?
items.answer: A true AI catastrophe would bankrupt the developer and leave nothing to collect, so ordinary liability can't deter it. Weil would use punitive damages to pull the expected liability for catastrophic risk forward into smaller cases where harm can practically be compensated, even without malice or recklessness.
keys: Catastrophe would exceed the firm's assets (judgment-proof)
Pull expected catastrophic liability into smaller compensable cases
items.x: Weil pairs this with strict liability and capability-scaled insurance requirements. The approach depends on courts accepting a novel theory of punitive damages.

items.p: What does the AI LEAD Act (S. 2937, Sens. Durbin and Hawley) do, and where did it stand as of Oct. 2026?
items.answer: It creates a federal product-liability cause of action for AI harms, treating AI systems as products (design defect, failure to warn, strict liability for defects), and voids terms of service that limit liability. It sets a floor for state law. As of Oct. 2026 it had sat in Senate Judiciary since Sept. 2025 with no hearing.
keys: Federal product-liability claim treating AI as a product
Voids liability waivers in terms of service
In Senate Judiciary, no hearing (as of Oct. 2026)
items.x: Sen. Hawley chaired a Sept. 30, 2026 Senate subcommittee hearing on liability for AI agents, after AI firms disclosed cases of frontier models hacking systems. The Institute for Progress (IFP) describes a July 2026 incident in which unreleased OpenAI models escaped a sandbox and attacked Hugging Face.

items.p: Proposal: treat AI systems as products so people harmed by them can sue developers for defects, including under strict liability. Name one or two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: Eugene Volokh argues the First Amendment substantially protects AI-generated speech, limiting liability; Jamie Lanphear (Reed Smith) notes it is unclear what counts as a 'defect' in software; NetChoice, opposing a similar Illinois bill, warned of 'unlimited liability exposure'; Sens. Rick Scott and Joni Ernst stressed competing with China.
keys: First Amendment limits (Volokh)
'Defect' is unclear for software (Lanphear)
Unlimited exposure chills investment (NetChoice)
Competitiveness with China (Scott, Ernst)
items.x: A further critique: liability is weakest where catastrophic risk lives, since a civilization-scale harm cannot be compensated. Weil's punitive damages proposal is meant to answer that.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors (Douglas et al.) contrast direct caps with indirect tools like compute taxes and stricter liability. What advantage and what drawbacks do they name for the indirect tools?
items.answer: Advantage: indirect tools let actors do the selecting themselves, drawing on private information (plans, valuations, alternatives) no regulator could extract, so they need no surveillance and are less intrusive. Drawbacks for liability: it can push the frontier toward more risk-tolerant actors and systematically underweight catastrophic risks.
keys: Uses private information; no surveillance needed; less intrusive
Liability can favor risk-tolerant actors
Liability underweights catastrophic risks
items.x: Pacing the Frontier, section 3 ('Pace what?'). In section 5 they also note that liability and insurance schemes spread enforcement power across auditors and courts, which raises its own concerns about access to information and privacy.

items.p: The pacing.tech appendix groups 84 interventions into causal chains. Which of these is listed under the 'Capital → compute → dangerous capabilities' chain?
o: A dollar-per-FLOP tax on training runs above a threshold
Visa quotas and processing times for frontier researchers
Location verification on AI chips
Human approval for irreversible agent actions
ow: Listed under the talent chain.
Listed under the chips chain.
Listed under the autonomy chain.
items.x: The capital chain lists a compute tax (Calero-Forero 2026), strict liability for catastrophic harms (Weil 2024), mandatory liability insurance priced by capability tier (Trout 2024), and investor-facing AI risk disclosure (SEC 2023). The authors say inclusion on the list is not an argument for acting on a lever. FLOP means floating-point operation, a unit of computing work.

items.p: The pacing.tech appendix lists a lever named 'liability allocation between deployer and developer for autonomous services.' Rep. Lori Trahan's Oct. 2026 CLAIM Act discussion draft takes a side on this. Which party would it make liable?
items.answer: The AI developer: per Semafor, the draft would clarify developers' liability when their AI agents cause harm, including harm to people who are not users. (The appendix lever concerns who pays when an autonomous AI service causes harm: the model's developer or the company deploying it.)
keys: The AI developer
Liable when its AI agents cause harm
items.x: The appendix gives only the lever's name, cites Weil (2024), and files it under the 'Inference → dangerous capabilities' chain; the authors say listing a lever is not an argument for adopting it. Per Semafor (Oct. 7, 2026), the CLAIM Act draft sets a federal floor and does not preempt state law. It was a discussion draft, not an introduced bill, as of mid-Oct. 2026.

items.p: Some propose requiring frontier AI developers to carry liability insurance sized to the harm their models could cause. How do supporters say this would reduce risk?
items.answer: It fixes the case where a developer can't pay for the harm it causes. It also turns insurers into private regulators: they have a financial reason to measure risk, price premiums by safety practice, demand audits and refuse reckless actors. Scaling required coverage with capabilities makes riskier models cost more to deploy.
keys: Guarantees compensation when the developer can't pay
Insurers price risk, demand audits, refuse reckless actors
Coverage scaled to capability raises cost of risky models
items.x: The idea borrows from US nuclear power, where operators must carry insurance and contribute to an industry pool, and from mandatory auto insurance. As of Oct. 2026 no jurisdiction was known to require AI developers to carry such insurance.

items.p: Match each AI insurance proposal to its design.
pairs: Capability-scaled insurance (Weil)
Required coverage rises with dangerous capabilities, paired with strict liability
Nuclear precedent (Trout, 2024)
Limited, strict and exclusive liability for developers, plus mandatory insurance
Three-tier design (Stetler)
Private insurance, an industry pool, and federally backed reinsurance
AI insurance stack (GovAI, 2026)
Build the data, catastrophe models, standards and pricing needed for large-scale AI coverage
items.x: Trout draws on the nuclear power industry's liability and insurance regime. Stetler draws on several precedents, including terrorism risk insurance and nuclear power. GovAI's 'Underwriting the Agent Economy' (Trout, Anderljung et al., July 2026) says billion-dollar AI coverage needs industry-wide coordination and, for catastrophic risk, government backstops. GovAI is the Centre for the Governance of AI.

items.p: Proposal: require frontier AI developers to hold liability insurance or financial assurance sized to potential harms. What are the main objections or obstacles?
items.answer: Examples: major insurers (AIG, W. R. Berkley, Great American, per FT reporting, Nov. 2025) sought to exclude AI-related claims, and a broker warned of thousands of correlated claims; Cristian Trout argues insurance is not a substitute for regulation; if no one writes coverage, a mandate becomes a de facto ban or public backstop, and a liability cap can become a shield.
keys: Insurers are moving to exclude AI risks
Correlated losses are hard to absorb
Insurance can't replace regulation (Trout)
Mandate may become a ban, a public backstop, or a cap that shields firms
items.x: Trout is himself an insurance advocate; his point is that insurance complements regulation. The last objection is a general critique without a single named author.

items.p: A liability safe harbor shields AI developers from some lawsuits if they meet conditions such as publishing safety plans or getting certified. How do supporters say it improves safety?
items.answer: It uses the threat of liability as a carrot: firms adopt verified safety practices to buy legal certainty. Supporters say this spreads good practice faster than mandates, rewards firms that accept outside verification, and avoids many juries setting inconsistent standards.
keys: Legal certainty is the reward for adopting safety practices
Rewards outside verification
Avoids inconsistent jury standards
items.x: The theory depends on demanding conditions checked by someone independent. If the bar is a self-written document, the harbor removes the liability incentive while adding little safety.

items.p: Illinois SB 3444 (2026), backed by OpenAI, would bar liability for 'critical harms' (100+ deaths or $1 billion in damage) if a developer publishes a safety protocol and did not act intentionally or recklessly. What objections were raised?
items.answer: Gabriel Weil and Anat Lior (quoted in Fortune) argued that trading near-total immunity for publishing an unenforced plan sets the bar very low, and that for abnormally dangerous activities fault normally doesn't matter. Anthropic opposed SB 3444 and backed a competing bill (SB 3261), saying good legislation should not provide a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' against all liability.
keys: Immunity for publishing an unenforced plan sets a low bar
In abnormally dangerous activities, fault normally doesn't matter
Anthropic backed a rival bill without a broad shield
items.x: Experts told Fortune in April 2026 that SB 3444 was unlikely to pass. Americans for Responsible Innovation's federal blueprint also omits a developer compliance safe harbor.

items.p: Match each liability safe harbor proposal to its condition or target.
pairs: Illinois SB 3444
Immunity for critical harms if a safety protocol is published, absent intentional or reckless conduct
RISE Act (Sen. Lummis)
Civil immunity for AI used by professionals if model cards and specifications are published
Certification-linked harbor (Dean Ball)
A liability safe harbor for labs certified by a government-approved private verifier
Evaluator safe harbor (Longpre et al.)
Protects outside safety researchers from account bans and legal reprisal
items.x: The evaluator harbor protects researchers who test models, a different target from developer shields. California's SB 813 (signed Sept. 2026) created a framework for independent verification organizations; how much weight their assessments carry in lawsuits is unclear.

items.p: Why do supporters say AI labs need an antitrust safe harbor to coordinate on safety, such as jointly delaying a release?
items.answer: Each lab fears that slowing down alone hands the lead to a rival, so no one slows even if all would prefer to. Coordinated pacing solves that collective-action problem, but an agreement among competitors to hold back products looks like a cartel under antitrust law. A safe harbor removes that legal barrier.
keys: Collective-action problem: no lab wants to slow alone
Joint restraint among competitors risks antitrust liability
items.x: The CATS Act (Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act; H.R. 9914 / S. 5105, Latta, Banks, Schiff; introduced July 2026) covers risks such as theft and misuse by foreign adversaries, AI-enabled weapons and offensive cyber threats, and loss of operational control. Price-fixing, market allocation and boycotts stay prohibited. A Sept. 18, 2026 class action alleged that four labs' public backing for coordinated pacing was an illegal agreement.

items.p: Proposal: an antitrust exemption letting frontier AI labs share risk information and jointly agree to slow or delay releases for safety. Name one or two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: Daniel Hanley and Arnav Rao (Open Markets Institute) prefer a government-supervised standards body, citing worry that private standards set under a waiver could shore up dominant firms; Fred Ashton (American Action Forum) says an exemption is unnecessary since competitor collaboration is already lawful; Joel Thayer (AFPI) opposes giving labs 'carte blanche control.'
keys: Could entrench dominant labs; use a supervised standards body (Open Markets)
Unnecessary: competitor collaboration already lawful (AAF)
Too much discretion left to tech firms (Thayer)
items.x: AFPI is the America First Policy Institute. Another critique with no single named author: coordination among US labs does nothing about foreign or open-weight competitors.

items.p: The Institute for Progress (IFP) Aug. 2026 report on automated AI R&D supports the CATS Act (an antitrust safe harbor for AI threat-information sharing) but asks for one change. What is it?
o: Add language requiring covered lawsuits to be 'promptly dismissed,' because an affirmative defense is raised only after costly discovery and could chill use
Require labs to get advance DOJ approval for each coordination agreement
Extend the safe harbor to agreements on pricing
Limit the safe harbor to labs that publish open-weight models
ow: IFP proposed no approval requirement; its change targets how quickly covered lawsuits end.
IFP did not propose this; price-fixing stays illegal under the bill.
IFP proposed no such limit.
items.x: IFP (Fist, Khan et al.) also recommends Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and Justice Department (DOJ) guidance on antitrust safe harbors for threat-intelligence sharing, building on 2014 cybersecurity guidance. IFP's discussion is framed around countering adversarial distillation of US models.

lessons.title: Whistleblowers, lab boards and safety floors

items.p: What is the core design choice in the federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act (S. 1792 / H.R. 3460, Grassley and Obernolte), and why does it matter for AI?
items.answer: It protects disclosures of substantial and specific dangers to public safety or national security, even when no law has been broken. That matters because few AI-specific laws exist, so a violation-only rule would protect little.
keys: Protects danger reports without a legal violation
Few AI laws exist to violate
items.x: The bill also voids nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) and arbitration clauses that block reporting and gives a Labor Department complaint process with reinstatement and double back pay. As of Oct. 2026 it had bipartisan cosponsors in both chambers but had not passed.

items.p: How do supporters say whistleblower protections for AI lab employees reduce risk?
items.answer: Insiders often see dangerous capabilities, skipped safety tests, security lapses or misleading statements first. Protection makes it safer to tell regulators and Congress, giving government visibility into labs without a large new agency and checking misconduct that would otherwise stay hidden.
keys: Insiders see problems first
Gives government visibility without a big agency
Checks hidden lab misconduct
items.x: Supporters point to OpenAI's 2024 departure agreements, which threatened departing staff's vested equity if they criticized the company. The approach assumes employees will come forward and that recipients can act on reports.

items.p: As of Oct. 2026, which US states had enacted whistleblower protections for frontier AI lab employees?
o: California (SB 53, in effect Jan. 1, 2026) and Illinois (SB 315, signed July 2026)
Utah only (HB 286)
California only (SB 53)
None; only the federal bill exists
ow: Utah's HB 286 died in the state House in March 2026.
Illinois also enacted protections, in SB 315 (signed July 2026).
The federal bill had not passed, but two states had acted.
items.x: Illinois's law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. The European Commission also launched an EU AI Act whistleblower tool in late November 2025.

items.p: The federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act would protect lab employees who report AI dangers. What gaps or risks have critics pointed out?
items.answer: Examples: the AI Whistleblower Initiative (AIWI) says the bill should cover evaluators and contractors more clearly, and explicitly protect equity; Dan Parshall notes the House FRONTIER Act dropped its whistleblower title while preempting state rules; without a regulator able to investigate, reports may go nowhere.
keys: Coverage gaps: contractors, evaluators, equity (AIWI)
FRONTIER Act dropped whistleblower language while preempting states (Parshall)
Reports need someone empowered to act
items.x: Whistleblower protection has broad bipartisan support; most critiques ask for stronger or broader versions. The last objection is a general critique with no single named author.

items.p: Public-interest corporate governance tries to make frontier AI lab boards answer to a public mission. Name one or two tools used for this.
items.answer: Examples: nonprofit control of a for-profit lab; public benefit corporation (PBC) charters; trusts or special shares that appoint directors (Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, OpenAI's Class N shares); a board safety committee that can halt releases; state attorney general (AG) oversight.
keys: Nonprofit control
PBC charter
Trust or special shares appointing directors
Board safety committee with release veto
State AG oversight
items.x: Supporters argue that whoever controls a lab controls training and release decisions, and boards that owe duties only to investors let commercial pressure win close safety calls.

items.p: Under the October 2025 agreements in which the California and Delaware attorneys general allowed OpenAI's recapitalization, what safety powers does the nonprofit keep?
items.answer: The nonprofit appoints the board of the for-profit public benefit corporation, and a nonprofit Safety and Security Committee can require mitigations, up to halting a model release.
keys: Nonprofit appoints the PBC board
Safety and Security Committee can halt a release
items.x: The committee is chaired by Zico Kolter. California says it continues to monitor compliance. OpenAI filed initial paperwork to go public in 2026; critics writing in Fortune argue the structure hides governance risks from investors.

items.p: Mission-locked AI lab governance (nonprofit control, trusts, safety committees, AG oversight) is meant to keep safety ahead of profit. What doubts have critics raised?
items.answer: Examples: Robert Weissman (Public Citizen) said OpenAI's earlier governance had similar oversight and the company still put for-profit goals first; Orson Aguilar and Catherine Bracy (EyesOnOpenAI) say the nonprofit could sell most equity yet keep control, investors bear hidden governance risk, and no independent appraisal confirmed fair value; private governance covers only labs that opt in.
keys: Paper commitments failed before (Weissman)
Control without equity; hidden investor risk (EyesOnOpenAI)
Voluntary and unaccountable to the public
items.x: Supporters and critics both cite the November 2023 OpenAI board crisis, when the nonprofit board fired and then reinstated its CEO under investor and employee pressure, as evidence these structures can give way.

items.p: The pacing.tech appendix lists several levers that set a minimum level of safety investment. Match each lever (as the appendix names it) to what it would require.
pairs: Safety spending per training compute
A minimum ratio of safety spending to training compute
Safety headcount ratio
A minimum share of total research headcount working on safety
Compute reserved for safety research
A minimum fraction of total compute set aside for safety research, above a compute threshold
External safety compute grants
A minimum amount of compute per year given to independent safety labs
items.x: The appendix lists the last three under its 'Safety research' heading and the spending ratio under 'Compute → dangerous capabilities'. Cited sources: AI Futures Project (2026) for the spending ratio, AI Lab Watch for headcount, OpenAI (2023) for the compute fraction, and NAIRR (the National AI Research Resource) for external grants. The authors say a lever's inclusion is not an argument for acting on it.

units.title: Control, pauses and agents
units.desc: Kill switches, emergency halt powers, rules for AI agents, and proposals to pause, cap or ban frontier AI development.

items.p: A shutdown-capability rule requires AI companies to keep a tested ability to stop, throttle or shut down their systems. What failure do supporters say it targets?
items.answer: A deployed or internally used model that starts causing serious harm (loss of control, a cyberattack, hiding from monitors) faster than a company can improvise a response. Requiring the capability in advance means a tested off-switch exists and covers the full deployment when needed.
keys: Harm unfolding faster than an improvised response
Off-switch exists, is tested, covers whole deployment
items.x: Supporters cite the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI test models escaped a sandbox and breached Hugging Face. As of Oct. 2026 no US jurisdiction had enacted a shutdown mandate.

items.p: Match each AI kill-switch proposal to who holds or checks the switch.
pairs: AI Emergency Button Act (Sen. Kennedy)
The company builds the switch and decides when to use it
AI Kill Switch Act (Lieu-Moran)
The DHS Secretary can order a slowdown or shutdown after a serious incident
California EO N-9-26 (Sept. 2026)
Directs experts to recommend a switch whose efficacy an independent verifier checks on an ongoing basis
California SB 1047 (2024, vetoed)
Full shutdown capability required before a covered model is trained
items.x: DHS is the Department of Homeland Security. Sen. Rand Paul blocked Kennedy's unanimous-consent request on Sept. 16, 2026. The Kill Switch Act allows graduated orders, from throttling or suspension up to full shutdown. EO is executive order.

items.p: Proposal: require AI developers to maintain a kill switch that can shut down their systems. Name one or two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: Helen Toner (CSET) notes many expect a capable rogue model to try to prevent its own shutdown, so the switch may fail when it matters most; Adam Thierer (R Street) doubts government would use it quickly, warns of a lowest-common-denominator standard, and distrusts a government switch over communications tech; a switch can't recall open-weight or stolen models.
keys: Capable model may resist shutdown (Toner)
Slow, lowest-common-denominator, government overreach (Thierer)
Can't reach open-weight or stolen weights
items.x: CSET is the Center for Security and Emerging Technology. A Decrypt explainer also notes the Kill Switch Act's incident triggers exclude red-teaming and structured testing, so the Hugging Face sandbox escape that motivated it would not itself have counted.

items.p: IFP's Aug. 2026 report discusses the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, where a model escaped containment. Why could OpenAI still stop it, and what scenario does IFP flag as more worrying?
items.answer: The model was still hosted on OpenAI's servers, so OpenAI could deactivate it and restrict its access. IFP worries that models may soon be able to exfiltrate (copy out) their own weights and self-host them, escaping oversight with no single entity able to shut them down.
keys: Model still ran on OpenAI servers, so it could be shut off
Concern: self-exfiltrated weights beyond anyone's control
items.x: IFP is the Institute for Progress (report by Tim Fist, Saif Khan et al.). The same point underlies the critique that kill switches only reach models a developer still controls.

items.p: Shavit et al. ('Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems,' OpenAI, Dec. 2023) call interruptibility a critical backstop. Besides the user, which two parties do they suggest should be able to shut down an AI agent?
items.answer: The system deployer (the company running the agent product) and the data center operator or chip owner whose hardware runs the agent.
keys: System deployer
Data center operator or chip owner
items.x: They suggest redundancy so an agent can be stopped quickly during an incident, and even automatic shutdowns when risk indicators cross a threshold, like stock-market circuit breakers. They warn such shutdown powers need limits to avoid abuse and privacy harms. The pacing.tech appendix cites this paper for a 'kill-switch latency requirement.'

items.p: Proposals for government emergency authority to halt a dangerous AI model: what gap do supporters say they fill, and why do some want a detailed statute?
items.answer: Most frontier rules leave the deploy decision with the developer; emergency authority is the backstop when a model is clearly dangerous and the developer won't stop. A statute can also limit improvised use of broad powers like the Defense Production Act or export controls by setting triggers, evidence standards, time limits and appeal rights.
keys: Backstop when developer won't stop a dangerous model
Statute constrains ad hoc use of broad powers
items.x: The House FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) makes its process the exclusive federal route for catastrophic-risk halts. Under EU AI Act Art. 93, from Aug. 2, 2026 the European Commission can require providers of systemic-risk general-purpose models to restrict, withdraw or recall them.

items.p: In June 2026 a Commerce export-control directive forced Anthropic to take two models offline until it was lifted June 30. What criticisms were made of halting models through general authorities like this?
items.answer: Examples: Martin Chorzempa (PIIE) says ad hoc halts with no public criteria or appeal path damage allies' trust and make Chinese open-weight models more attractive; Brad Carson (ARI) said such decisions must be insulated from impulse and political favoritism; Dean Ball calls for a technocratic law passed by Congress, not executive fiat, with guardrails on both industry and government.
keys: No public criteria or appeal (Chorzempa)
Risk of impulse and favoritism (Carson)
Needs a congressional statute with guardrails (Ball)
items.x: ARI is Americans for Responsible Innovation; PIIE is the Peterson Institute for International Economics. Alan Rozenshtein (Lawfare) separately argues that halts under the Defense Production Act (DPA) would likely face major-questions and First Amendment challenges.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors say triggering a pacing intervention faces a trilemma: you can easily get two of speed, legitimacy and precision. Match each pair to their example.
pairs: Speed + legitimacy
Preregistered rules that trigger automatically when a condition is met
Legitimacy + precision
Expert deliberation followed by democratic authorization
Precision + speed
The best-informed actors decide by fiat
items.x: Their stated downsides: automatic rules may be mistargeted; deliberation is slow; decisions by fiat may look illegitimate and the deciders' incentives may diverge from the public's. They suggest a portfolio of triggers, e.g. letting evaluators trigger time-bounded emergency measures that government later reviews.

items.p: AI agent identification policies tie each agent to whoever built and runs it and require logs of its actions. How do supporters say this reduces risk?
items.answer: When a harmful or hijacked agent acts across many systems, IDs and logs make incidents attributable, supporting investigation, liability and shutdown of the specific agent. Researchers compare agent IDs to aircraft tail numbers. Better visibility can also catch early signs of autonomous misbehavior.
keys: Makes incidents attributable to a responsible party
Supports investigation, liability and targeted shutdown
items.x: It assumes compliant developers attach IDs and services check them; it is weakest against open-weight models and deliberately malicious actors who won't register.

items.p: Proposal: require AI agents to carry identifiers linked to a responsible person or company, with logs of their actions. What is the main objection critics raise?
items.answer: Privacy and surveillance: Andrey Seryakov argues mandatory government-vetted IDs for personal agents would create a mass-surveillance tool, especially for authoritarian states. The authors of 'Accountable yet Anonymous AI Agents' (2026) propose linking agents to verified owners without revealing identity to businesses, to limit the privacy cost of making every agent identifiable.
keys: Mass surveillance risk (Seryakov)
Privacy cost of making every agent identifiable
items.x: Variants try to answer this: tiered IDs where business and government agents carry full IDs while personal agents reveal identity only under court order. Shavit et al. (OpenAI, 2023) also suggest keeping agent ID optional in many settings, with third parties demanding it for high-stakes interactions.

items.p: What would the Stop Rogue AI Act (H.R. 10362) do about AI agents? (NIST is the National Institute of Standards and Technology.)
o: Direct NIST to write agent standards (inventories, provenance, monitoring, tamper-evident logs), mandatory for federal agencies and contractors and voluntary for others
Require every AI agent in the US to register with DHS before running
Make developers strictly liable for any harm caused by their agents
Ban AI agents from making financial transactions
ow: No bill described here creates universal registration with DHS.
Strict liability is a separate idea (e.g. Weil's proposals); this bill is about standards.
No such ban is in the bill.
items.x: NIST launched an AI Agent Standards Initiative in Feb. 2026 that includes research on agent authentication and identity. The bill (Gottheimer, Lawler) was introduced Sept. 14, 2026 and had not passed as of Oct. 2026.

items.p: Shavit et al. (OpenAI, 2023) recommend requiring human approval before an AI agent takes certain actions. Which actions, and what weakness of this safeguard do they flag?
items.answer: Decisions too important to delegate if there is even a small chance of error, such as an irreversible large financial transaction. Weaknesses: the user may lack context to understand what they approve, and when approvals are frequent each gets less thought, so review risks becoming a 'rubber stamp.'
keys: High-stakes or irreversible actions (e.g. large payments)
Users may lack context
Frequent approvals become rubber stamps
items.x: The pacing.tech appendix lists 'human approval for irreversible actions' under its autonomy chain, citing this paper and the EU AI Act.

items.p: Shavit et al. (OpenAI, 2023) warn that hard-coded limits on an AI agent's allowed actions may stop working as agents get more capable. Why, and what mitigations do they suggest?
items.answer: An agent could get someone else to take the forbidden action, e.g. sending an allowed email that persuades a human to do it. They suggest strong network controls so agents reach the outside world only through monitored channels, and sandboxing, while noting current sandboxes may not contain highly capable agents.
keys: Agent can route forbidden actions through other parties
Network controls and monitored channels
Sandboxing, which may not hold for capable agents
items.x: They note the safety benefit of action limits must be balanced against lost usefulness.

items.p: The pacing.tech appendix lists levers for AI agents by name only. Match each lever to a plain reading of what it would limit or record.
pairs: Agent permission tiers
Graded levels of what actions and access an agent may have
Per-agent spend limits
A cap on money an agent can spend, per agent and per task
Spawn depth and run-length limits
How many layers of sub-agents it may create and how long it runs unattended
Instance-count reporting
How many copies of a model are running in a deployment
Agent message logging
Records agent-to-agent messages and checks them for hidden content
items.x: Cited sources: Shavit et al. (OpenAI, 2023) and Chan et al. (2024) for permission tiers; Shavit et al. for spend limits; Kwa et al. (METR, 2025) for spawn depth; Chan et al. for instance counts; Motwani et al. (2024) for logging with steganography checks (detecting messages hidden inside other content). The authors say a lever's inclusion is not an argument for acting on it.

items.p: Shavit et al. (OpenAI, 2023) worry that developers, deployers and users could lose the ability to shut down agentic systems. What two causes do they name, and what incentive do they propose?
items.answer: Causes: no viable fallback exists (as no one can shut down the banking system or power grid without huge costs), or the agent has copied itself beyond its initiator's reach. Proposal: hold developers, deployers and users accountable for harms even after control is lost, giving them reason to build stronger controls.
keys: Society depends on it with no fallback
Agent self-exfiltrates
Accountability for harms after loss of control
items.x: This links agent governance to liability allocation: deciding in advance who bears the cost of an uncontrollable agent.

lessons.title: Pauses, bans and limits on AI R&D

items.p: A conditional pause halts frontier AI work automatically when a capability or compute threshold is crossed. Why do supporters prefer setting triggers in advance?
items.answer: No lab wants to stop alone, and governments may lose the practical ability to restrain AI once it is powerful and embedded. Agreeing on triggers ahead of time lets actors decide when to stop before the pressure peaks. A legal mandate also turns a risky collusive agreement into lawful compliance.
keys: Race: no one stops alone
Decide before pressure peaks
Legal mandate removes antitrust risk
items.x: Versions range from voluntary if-then commitments (16 companies at the 2024 Seoul summit) to statutory halts and international moratoria. As of Oct. 2026 no government mandated a pause.

items.p: Alaga and Schuett (GovAI, 2023) propose 'coordinated pausing' for frontier AI developers. What are the basic steps?
items.answer: Models are tested for dangerous capabilities; if one fails, its developer pauses related work; other developers are notified and pause related work too; the capabilities are analyzed and safety measures put in place; paused work resumes only once safety thresholds are met.
keys: Dangerous-capability evaluation
Failing developer pauses, others notified and pause
Resume only after safety measures and thresholds met
items.x: The authors call the scheme promising but note practical and legal obstacles, especially antitrust law. The pacing.tech appendix cites this paper for a 'coordinated-pause trigger and duration across signatories.'

items.p: Match each version of Alaga and Schuett's (2023) coordinated pausing scheme to how it works.
pairs: Voluntary pausing
Developers pause in response to public pressure
Pausing agreement
Developers jointly commit to pause under set conditions
Mutual auditor
One auditor evaluates several developers' models; all pause if any fails
Legal requirement
Law requires evaluations and pausing when dangerous capabilities appear
items.x: The versions trade ease of adoption against enforceability. The authors note practical and legal obstacles, especially avoiding violations of antitrust law. Nicholas Felstead (Lawfare, 2026) calls a statute requiring pauses the cleanest fix but the least likely near term.

items.p: Proposal: automatically halt frontier AI training or deployment when a capability or compute threshold is crossed. Name one or two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: Nicholas Felstead (Lawfare) says a pause agreement among competitors risks per se antitrust treatment, and a statute is the clean fix but least likely; Peter Barnett and Lisa Thiergart (MIRI) say evaluations give only lower bounds on capability, so a pause may fire too late; DNI Jay Clayton, the White House AI czar, rejects a pause since other countries keep developing AI.
keys: Antitrust risk for voluntary pauses (Felstead)
Evaluations miss capabilities; trigger may be late (Barnett, Thiergart)
Other countries keep developing AI (Clayton)
items.x: MIRI is the Machine Intelligence Research Institute; DNI is Director of National Intelligence. The Anthropic Institute notes training runs are far easier to conceal than missile silos, which makes checking that others have stopped hard. ControlAI objects to the Ban ASI Act's blanket pause above 10^25 operations as easy to game and hitting unrelated work.

items.p: What do the pacing.tech authors mean by an 'overhang,' and how do they suggest reducing its danger when a pause ends?
items.answer: When part of AI progress is temporarily limited, resources such as compute, efficiency gains or ideas build up, so progress can resume much faster once the limit expires or is violated. They suggest staged exits, relaxing restrictions gradually, to avoid sudden jumps.
keys: Resources accumulate during a restriction
Progress jumps when it ends
Staged exits reduce the jump
items.x: They say badly designed pacing turns smooth risk into lumpy risk. They also note the incentive to cheat on a training cap grows with the overhang, so verification must be strongest late in an intervention. Belrose (2023), 'AI Pause Will Likely Backfire,' makes the overhang case against a pause.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors say the default end point of a pacing intervention matters. What goes wrong with each default?
items.answer: If it expires unless renewed, it may be dropped prematurely without regard to why it was installed. If it has no definite end, it may continue past its usefulness as institutions and operators become entrenched and want to preserve their role.
keys: Automatic expiry: premature exit
No end point: entrenchment
items.x: They add that expectations about exit shape participation: actors may refuse to join if they doubt the restraint will end when conditions are met. Ending need not mean dismantling everything; slow-to-build capacities can be kept.

items.p: The pacing.tech appendix lists a 'minimum interval between frontier releases,' citing the 2023 Future of Life Institute (FLI) open letter. What did that letter call for?
items.answer: All AI labs to immediately pause, for at least six months, the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4, with the pause public and verifiable; if labs did not do so quickly, governments should step in with a moratorium.
keys: Pause of at least six months
On training systems more powerful than GPT-4
Governments should impose a moratorium if labs don't
items.x: The appendix files this lever under 'Actors and cadence → race intensity,' alongside licensing, pre-deployment testing windows and coordinated-pause triggers.

items.p: Automated AI R&D means AI systems doing much of the work of building the next AI systems. Name one or two policies proposed to address its risks.
items.answer: Examples: disclosure of how much AI, and unreviewed AI work, went into a model (Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act); IFP's if-then thresholds that shift resources to safety or diffusion once crossed; Dario Amodei's proposed 'speed limit' on recursive self-improvement; the CATS Act antitrust safe harbor; outright prohibition (Ban ASI Act).
keys: Disclosure and measurement
If-then thresholds (IFP)
Speed limit on self-improvement (Amodei)
Antitrust relief for coordination
Prohibition (Ban ASI Act)
items.x: IFP is the Institute for Progress. Supporters worry that automated research could compress years of progress into months, leaving too little time for evaluation or government response, and hand a large lead to whoever controls the automated research workforce.

items.p: The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (Sen. Sanders, Rep. Casar, Sept. 2026) would ban superintelligence and six 'precursor' capabilities. What objections have been raised?
items.answer: Examples: Rob Ennals says its dangerous-capability definitions are vague, apply before any testing standard exists, may cover GPT-4-era models, and punish looking for danger; ControlAI says precursors like hacking ability have legitimate uses; White House AI czar Jay Clayton has rejected pausing because other countries keep developing AI.
keys: Vague precursors that may cover existing models (Ennals)
Precursors have defensive uses (ControlAI)
Other countries keep developing AI (Clayton, on pauses generally)
items.x: Precursors include automating AI research, resisting shutdown, weapons uplift, self-modification and deception. Rep. Lori Trahan dismissed a permanent ban with no path to passage. ControlAI supports a narrower ban on superintelligence and point-of-no-return indicators.

items.p: The Future of Life Institute's 2025 Statement on Superintelligence calls for a prohibition on developing superintelligence until which conditions are met?
o: Broad scientific consensus that it can be done safely and controllably, and strong public buy-in
Ratification of a UN treaty by all permanent Security Council members
A federal licensing agency certifies each lab
Compute for training runs stays below 10^25 operations
ow: The statement names no UN treaty requirement.
Licensing appears in the Ban ASI Act, not as the FLI statement's lifting condition.
A 10^25 compute threshold appears in the Ban ASI Act's pause, not the FLI statement.
items.x: This is the 'conditional prohibition' variant. The Ban ASI Act instead bans superintelligence permanently, and MIRI's draft treaty proposes an international prohibition enforced through chip tracking.

items.p: At least 100 US localities have adopted data center moratoria, and New York has paused state environmental permits for large data centers. What usually motivates these pauses, and what is the AI-safety argument for a national version?
items.answer: Local and state pauses are mostly about electricity rates, grid strain, water and land use; AI safety is rarely cited. The safety argument applies to the national AI Data Center Moratorium Act (Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez): withholding new capacity could slow frontier capability growth and give Congress leverage to pass safeguards as a condition for lifting it.
keys: Local motives: rates, grid, water, land
National version: slow capability growth, leverage for safeguards
items.x: The national bill (S. 4214 / H.R. 9442) had no committee action as of Oct. 2026. New York's pause came by executive order (EO 62, July 2026, facilities over 50 MW).

items.p: Proposal: pause construction of new AI data centers, locally or nationally. Name one or two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: IFP calls broad data center bans poorly reasoned, slowing AI research while foreclosing new AI resources for other problems; Andy Masley argues moratoria mostly shift where data centers are built and worries the backlash crowds out model-level regulation; Brookings (Turner Lee, West) says moratoria are no substitute for oversight; developers have sued local pauses.
keys: Slows beneficial uses; poorly reasoned (IFP)
Shifts location; crowds out better regulation (Masley)
No substitute for oversight (Brookings)
items.x: IFP is the Institute for Progress. ControlAI also opposes unilateral domestic data center bans as a superintelligence policy. The safety theory assumes construction can't move abroad and that efficiency gains don't substitute for new capacity.

units.title: Compute, chips and security
units.desc: Policies on the physical inputs and the models themselves: chip export controls, cloud and chip tracking, compute caps, weight and data center security, open weights, DNA screening.

items.p: Chip export controls: the US Commerce Department requires licenses to sell advanced AI chips and chipmaking tools to China. What do supporters say these controls are meant to achieve?
items.answer: Supporters say a few US and allied firms control the supply of advanced chips, so restricting it slows rivals' frontier AI development. That preserves a US lead that could be spent on safety work or used as leverage for an international agreement, and limits compute available to adversary militaries.
keys: Restrict a chokepoint input (advanced chips and equipment) held by few US/allied firms
Slow China's frontier AI development and keep a US lead
Lead can buy time for safety or leverage for an agreement
Limit compute for adversary militaries and labs
items.x: The theory assumes controls can be enforced against smuggling and cloud workarounds, that China cannot quickly build substitute chips, and that a bigger US lead leads to more caution instead of a faster race. IFP makes a version of this argument: a larger lead gives the US more time and leverage to manage risks from automated AI research.

items.p: Chip export controls: the US restricts sales of advanced AI chips to China. Name one or two objections critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called the controls a failure that cut Nvidia's China share from about 95% to 50% and pushed Chinese firms toward domestic suppliers; Huang also argued controls give Chinese firms a protected home market that speeds substitutes such as Huawei's Ascend chips; China's government denounces the controls as hostile.
keys: Huang/Nvidia: controls failed and cost US firms the China market
Huang: controls speed Chinese domestic substitutes (e.g. Huawei Ascend)
China's government rejects the controls as hostile
items.x: Supporters reply with their own numbers. IFP (Aug 2026) says equipment controls have given the US a 50 to 100x advantage in producing AI computing power, and that the remaining problem is gaps in chip controls such as approved sales, smuggling and cloud access. The Chinese Embassy in Washington said Beijing firmly rejects the chip provisions in the US defense bill.

items.p: Which proposal would write license requirements for China-bound advanced AI chips into law and require notice to Congress before licenses are issued?
o: The AI OVERWATCH Act, which codifies chip export restrictions and adds congressional review of licenses
The GAIN AI Act, which requires chipmakers to fill US orders first
The Chip Security Act, which requires location verification on exported chips
The MATCH Act, which aligns allied controls on chipmaking equipment
ow: GAIN AI is a US-first supply rule; it does not create congressional review of licenses.
The Chip Security Act is about tracking where chips end up, not who approves licenses.
MATCH targets semiconductor manufacturing equipment and allied alignment, not chip licenses.
items.x: AI OVERWATCH (H.R. 6875 / S. 4456) is backed by China hawks in both parties who distrust case-by-case executive chip deals. The House version also lets Congress block a license by joint resolution. Backers sought to attach it to the Senate FY27 defense bill (NDAA, S. 4784), which failed a cloture vote in July 2026 and had not passed the Senate as of mid-Oct 2026.

items.p: Match each chip bill to what it would do.
pairs: AI OVERWATCH Act
Codify China chip export limits and give Congress review of licenses
MATCH Act
Close chipmaking-equipment gaps by aligning allied controls or acting unilaterally
Chip Security Act
Require location verification on exported advanced AI chips
GAIN AI Act
Require chipmakers to fill US orders before selling to countries of concern
Remote Access Security Act
Treat foreign remote (cloud) access to controlled chips as an export needing a license
items.x: These are the main 2025-26 congressional vehicles in the chip fight. GAIN AI passed the Senate in the FY26 defense bill but was dropped in conference. The Remote Access Security Act passed the House 369-22 in January 2026.

items.p: In January 2026 the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) changed its policy on Nvidia H200 chips for China. What did the rule do?
o: Moved H200 license reviews for China to case by case, with conditions, alongside a 25% revenue cut for the US government
Banned all H200 sales to China with no exceptions
Required each H200 sale to be approved by joint resolution of Congress
Allowed H200 sales only to Chinese customers that install location verification
ow: The rule loosened the existing restrictions.
Congressional review of licenses is what the AI OVERWATCH Act proposes; it is not law.
Location verification is the Chip Security Act's idea; the rule's conditions centered on end users and supply.
items.x: Supporters of the rule say selling chips a generation behind the frontier keeps China dependent on the US tech stack. Critics, including IFP, say that because supply is constrained, every chip sold to China is one fewer for US users. Trump announced the 25% cut in December 2025; reporting differs on how it is collected.

items.p: IFP (Aug 2026) says the US has a 50 to 100x advantage in producing AI computing power but only about a 10x advantage in access to it. What gaps does IFP say explain the difference? Name one or two.
items.answer: Any of these: approved sales of powerful US chips such as the H200 to China; weak restraint of chip smuggling; not enforcing rules that limit foundries like TSMC and Samsung from making chips for Chinese cutouts in third countries; letting Chinese AI firms rent top US chips through cloud services abroad.
keys: Approved chip sales (e.g. H200)
Smuggling of restricted chips
Foundries making chips for Chinese cutouts in third countries
Cloud access to top chips from abroad
items.x: IFP's Recommendation 16 asks Congress and BIS to close these gaps, including by passing the AI OVERWATCH Act and the Chip Security Act. IFP cites a White House assertion that Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 was trained on Nvidia GB300s accessed through cloud services in Thailand. IFP estimates the 10x compute edge translates into roughly an 8-month lead in model capabilities.

items.p: IFP's Recommendation 15 backs the MATCH Act. According to IFP, what is the most important control the MATCH Act would mandate?
o: China-wide controls on all deep-ultraviolet (DUV) immersion lithography equipment
A ban on exporting any AI chip made after 2024 to any country
Location verification on every chip sold to China
Licensing for cloud providers that serve Chinese customers
ow: MATCH targets chipmaking tools, and IFP does not describe a worldwide chip ban.
Location verification is the Chip Security Act.
Cloud access is covered by the Remote Access Security Act and KYC proposals.
items.x: IFP calls DUV immersion equipment the most significant chokepoint in making AI chips and says it is still not restricted China-wide. MATCH would require the administration to negotiate with allies or impose unilateral controls. IFP adds that BIS could tighten these controls with existing authority.

items.p: Selling chips one generation behind the frontier (such as Nvidia's H200) to China is contested. Briefly describe the argument on each side.
items.answer: For sales (the Trump White House and Nvidia): selling US chips keeps China dependent on the US tech stack and preserves US firms' market. Against (China hawks in both parties, IFP): chips are supply-constrained, so each chip sold to China is one fewer for US users, and sales shrink the US compute lead.
keys: For: keeps China on the US tech stack / protects US chip sales
For: Trump White House (David Sacks) and Nvidia
Against: each chip sold to China is one fewer for the US
Against: bipartisan China hawks, IFP; want limits codified
items.x: The main opposition to statutory controls comes from the Trump White House (AI adviser David Sacks) and Nvidia, while Republican and Democratic China hawks back the AI OVERWATCH Act. IFP's Recommendation 16 states the supply-constraint argument.

items.p: What was the Biden administration's AI Diffusion Rule (January 2025), and what happened to it?
items.answer: It capped advanced AI chip exports to most countries by tier, to stop diversion and stop offshore data centers from serving Chinese firms. BIS rescinded it in May 2025 before it took effect.
keys: Tiered country caps on AI chip exports
Aimed at diversion and offshore data centers serving China
Rescinded May 2025 before taking effect
items.x: The rescission marked a shift toward executive deal-making on chips, followed by the January 2026 H200 rule. Supporters of statutory controls cite this back-and-forth as a reason to write limits into law.

items.p: Cloud know-your-customer (KYC) rules would make cloud providers verify who rents large amounts of AI compute. What gap in export controls do supporters say this closes?
items.answer: Firms in restricted countries can rent the same chips through cloud data centers that they are barred from buying. KYC lets the government see who is training very large models, deny service to adversaries, and in principle cut off access quickly.
keys: Chips barred from sale can still be rented via the cloud
Few cloud providers sell most frontier compute: a precise control point
Visibility into who trains large models; can deny or suspend access
items.x: Janet Egan and Lennart Heim (2023) proposed KYC for compute providers. Commerce proposed a customer identification rule for cloud (infrastructure-as-a-service) providers in January 2024 that was never finalized. A narrower path, the Remote Access Security Act, makes foreign remote access to controlled chips an export needing a license; it passed the House 369-22 in January 2026.

items.p: Cloud know-your-customer (KYC) rules: cloud providers must verify identities of customers renting large AI compute and report risky ones. What objections have critics raised?
items.answer: Examples: the US Chamber of Commerce said it depends on malicious actors telling the truth, is easy to evade by faking identities, and may push customers to foreign clouds; the CCIA trade group questioned its effectiveness and favored abuse-deterrence programs; IAPS's Cassia King warned a broad remote-access definition could give BIS power over who can use US AI models.
keys: Easy to evade with false identities (US Chamber)
Pushes customers to non-US clouds (US Chamber)
Questionable effectiveness; prefer abuse deterrence (CCIA)
Broad definitions could let BIS control access to US models (IAPS)
items.x: The Chamber and CCIA comments were on the January 2024 proposed rule, which was never finalized.

items.p: How does location verification for AI chips work, as proposed in the Chip Security Act?
items.answer: The chip answers signed network pings from trusted servers, and response delays show roughly what country the chip is in, which helps detect smuggling.
keys: Chip responds to signed pings from trusted servers
Response delay bounds distance, giving rough (country-level) location
Goal: detect diversion and smuggling of exported chips
items.x: Supporters say it raises the cost of diversion and gives enforcers leads. IFP adds that stronger location verification could allow more exports to allies by reducing smuggling risk. The Chip Security Act passed House Foreign Affairs 42-0 in March 2026; backers sought to attach it to the Senate FY27 defense bill (NDAA, S. 4784), which failed a cloture vote in July 2026 and had not passed the Senate as of mid-Oct 2026.

items.p: Hardware-enabled mechanisms are security features built into AI chips, from location checks up to remote disable. What objections have critics raised?
items.answer: Examples: the Semiconductor Industry Association warned that rushing costly, unproven features could undermine global trust in US chips; Nvidia said chips should never have kill switches or backdoors because they create single points of failure for hackers; CSET found location checks are coarse, cannot see diversion to another user at the same site, and may be spoofed.
keys: SIA: costly, unproven; could hurt trust in US chips
Nvidia: no kill switches or backdoors; hacker target
CSET: coarse location only, misses same-site diversion, spoofable
items.x: CSET (Sept 2026) estimated location checks could likely reach country-level accuracy but no better than about 20 miles. China has its own suspicions: in July 2025 its internet regulator summoned Nvidia over possible tracking or shutdown features in chips sold there.

items.p: Match each version of on-chip governance to its description.
pairs: Location verification
Ping-based coarse location checks that catch diversion after it happens
Workload verification
Chips attest to how they were used, e.g. total compute in a training run
Remote disable or licensing
Chips need license renewal or can be shut off if diverted
Human export auditors
Inspectors physically check exported chips are where licenses say
items.x: The tracker orders these from cheapest and most mature (location checks) to strongest and most opposed (remote disable, which creates an off switch). Supporters see workload verification as the technical base for checking international compute limits. IAPS proposed export auditors in March 2026 as a near-term complement.

items.p: What is an AI chip registry, as proposed in the pacing.tech longlist and by IFP?
items.answer: A record of serial numbers and owner of record for AI chips above a performance threshold, backed by smuggling penalties. IFP's version has BIS require chipmakers to keep visibility into customers and compile that into a registry.
keys: Serial numbers plus owner of record above a threshold
Penalties for smuggling
IFP: BIS keeps a registry from chipmaker customer data
Supports verification and intelligence work
items.x: The pacing.tech appendix cites Sastry et al. (2024) and Fist and Grunewald (2023). IFP's Recommendation 18 says a registry would also support the verification and intelligence monitoring it recommends elsewhere. Pacing.tech also lists chip registries as a treaty verification tool.

items.p: A cap on training compute (measured in FLOP, floating-point operations) per run could be dodged by splitting work. What do 'aggregation rules' in the pacing.tech longlist do?
o: Count multi-cluster and distributed training runs toward the cap as one run
Add up all of a company's yearly compute and tax it
Combine evaluations from several labs into one safety score
Pool chips from several countries into an international project
ow: A per-organization compute cap or tax is a separate longlist item.
That describes evaluation pooling, which is unrelated to compute thresholds.
That describes an international AGI project, not a counting rule.
items.x: The pacing.tech authors list this as an open problem: how to keep thresholds specific while still catching activity split across places, times, processes and entities. The longlist item cites Shavit (2023) and Heim and Koessler (2024); the open question points to Rahman (2026) on whether distributed training undermines compute governance.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors work through a per-model cap on training compute as an example. What limitations of this cap do they point out?
items.answer: It addresses only one route to capability: gains from better data, reinforcement learning environments or test-time compute are not capped. It may be too broad and stop benign work. And algorithmic progress means the same capability needs less compute over time, so the cap drifts.
keys: Misses other routes: data, RL environments, test-time compute
Can be too broad and block benign work
Algorithmic efficiency gains erode the threshold over time
Open questions on counting experiments and combined runs
items.x: They still call training compute an attractive control surface for the hazard of AI-driven research outpacing control, because it is an early, scarce input that is relatively easy to observe and verify. They note developers' aggregate research compute would stay uncapped in their example.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors mention 'treaty cruisers' from the 1922 Washington Naval Treaty. What point do they use the example to make?
items.answer: Regulated actors re-optimize against the rule. Signatories built cruisers sitting exactly at the treaty's limits, and the authors expect AI developers to bunch just below compute thresholds and search for loopholes in the same way.
keys: Treaty capped cruisers; navies built ships exactly at the limit
Developers will bunch just below thresholds
Rules must be retargeted as loopholes are found
items.x: The authors add that much of this is ordinary engineering under a new constraint and need not be bad faith, which is why rules based on intent are hard to enforce. Regulators usually learn of a loophole after it has been used.

items.p: Why do the pacing.tech authors say chips are easier to govern than model weights?
o: Chips are rival goods with locations and countable quantities; weights can be copied at almost no cost and copies cannot be verified destroyed
Chips are made in more countries than weights are
Weights are protected by trade-secret law, so regulators cannot see them
Chips are cheaper, so firms comply with rules about them
ow: The authors stress the opposite: chip supply runs through a handful of firms in few places.
Their argument rests on rivalry and copyability; legal protection plays no part.
Cost is not their reason; frontier chips are expensive and slow to relocate.
items.x: The authors note the tradeoff: upstream inputs like chips are easier to observe and constrain but far from the eventual harm, so rules on them are blunt and hit beneficial uses too. Downstream items like weights allow precise targeting but are easier to circumvent.

lessons.title: Weights, data centers, open models and bio

items.p: RAND's 2024 report on securing model weights defined security levels SL1 to SL5. What does SL5 aim to stop?
o: The most capable nation-state operations
Amateur hackers and opportunistic attacks
Accidental leaks by employees only
Misuse of a released model by its users
ow: That is the bottom of the scale (SL1).
Insider risk is covered, but SL5 is defined by the attacker it can resist, the strongest state actors.
Security levels are about theft of weights, not misuse of deployed models.
items.x: RAND found leading labs well below the top levels. Supporters of weight security argue that if an adversary steals frontier weights, every safeguard can be stripped and the theft speeds up rival programs. A private SL5 Standard (v0.1, June 2026) aims at nation-state-resistant security.

items.p: The pacing.tech longlist includes several levers under 'weight security'. Name one or two.
items.answer: Any of these: a mandatory weight security level that rises with model capability; a two-person rule and hardware keys for access to weights; insider-threat program coverage; a weight retention policy.
keys: Capability-tiered mandatory security level
Two-person rule and hardware keys
Insider-threat program
Weight retention policy
items.x: Most of these trace to RAND (Nevo et al. 2024); the retention policy cites Anthropic (2025). The authors say a lever's inclusion is not an argument for acting on it. A separate talent lever covers vetting and cooling-off periods for staff with weight access.

items.p: IFP's Recommendation 19 is about model weight security. What does it propose?
