items.answer: The Department of War, intelligence agencies, CAISI (the Center for AI Standards and Innovation) and research centers such as RAND should set consensus guidelines for protecting weights up to SL4 or SL5, and prototype an SL4 or SL5 government cluster where highly sensitive industry weights could be moved if needed.
keys: Consensus guidelines to reach SL4/SL5 against nation-states
Prototype a highly secure government compute cluster
Sensitive weights could be transferred there if needed
items.x: IFP argues weights are the 'crown jewels' and labs cannot currently stop state-backed theft. It cites RAND estimates of 37 to 50 million dollars for a proof-of-concept secure facility and 277 to 345 million dollars for an enterprise-scale one. IFP also says such a cluster could test models with less risk of escape.

items.p: As of October 2026, what did California SB 53 require on model weight security, and did any US law set a minimum security level?
items.answer: SB 53 requires large frontier developers to describe in their published frameworks how they secure unreleased model weights. No US law sets a minimum security level. A Senate FY27 defense bill (NDAA) provision requiring defense AI contractors to report theft or tampering attempts had not become law.
keys: CA SB 53: disclose weight security practices
No law sets a minimum security level
Senate FY27 NDAA contractor reporting provision not enacted
items.x: Options beyond disclosure include capability-tiered mandatory levels (proposed by RAND), insider-threat reporting through contracts, and government security partnerships. The SL5 Standard's authors warn SL5 requires measures far from current practice, close to government capabilities, which may be infeasible on a short timeline without a direct government role.

items.p: IFP (June 2026) proposed a 'speed-for-security bargain' for AI data centers. How would it work?
items.answer: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) would give faster grid interconnection to large AI loads that are curtailable and meet strong security controls, and would direct the grid standards body NERC to write binding security standards for them.
keys: Trade faster grid hookups for security controls
FERC fast-tracks interconnection for compliant AI loads
NERC writes binding security standards
items.x: The logic is leverage: builders need power, land and permits, so government can attach security conditions without a new agency. The author, Ben Schifman, notes binding NERC standards would not take effect until around 2028, after much capacity is built, so interim controls are needed. As of Oct 2026, no binding security standard applies to private US AI data centers.

items.p: Open-weight AI release is contested. Which groups have argued against new restrictions, and on what grounds? Name one or two.
items.answer: Examples: NTIA's 2024 report recommended no new restrictions, saying evidence of marginal risk over closed models was thin; the Center for Democracy & Technology applauded that finding; about 25 companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and Meta signed a July 2026 letter urging no premature restrictions. Supporters of openness also say it spreads power away from a few labs.
keys: NTIA (2024): evidence does not yet justify limits
CDT backed NTIA's finding
July 2026 industry letter (~25 firms) against premature limits
Openness spreads power and helps security research
items.x: On the other side, FAR.AI research shows fine-tuning can efficiently strip safeguards from models whose weights are available, which supporters of capability-gated limits cite. Anthropic did not sign the July 2026 letter; its CEO said that month he does not support an open-weight ban (Axios).

items.p: Match each open-weight policy option to its description.
pairs: Capability-threshold restriction
No open release above a defined dangerous-capability line
Same testing for open and closed
Mandatory safety tests for capable models however released
Staged release
API, then research access, then weights, as evidence builds
Country-of-origin limits
Restrict US use of models from Chinese labs
Open-source protection
Shield open models from frontier obligations
items.x: Proponents: Seger et al. (2023) for thresholds; Anthropic (July 2026) for equal testing; Irene Solaiman for the release gradient; administration discussion after Kimi K3 for country limits; the 2025 AI Action Plan and July 2026 industry letter for protection. As of Oct 2026 no US or EU law restricts open-weight release.

items.p: Mandatory DNA synthesis screening would require companies that make synthetic DNA to check orders and customers. How do supporters say it reduces AI-enabled bioweapon risk?
items.answer: AI may lower the knowledge barrier to designing pathogens, but a design still needs physical DNA. Synthesis is a narrow industry, so screening there is a chokepoint that works no matter which AI model was used, including open-weight ones.
keys: Designs still need physical DNA to become weapons
Synthesis is a concentrated chokepoint
Works regardless of the AI model, including open-weight
items.x: The Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act (S. 3741, Cotton-Klobuchar) would require all providers to screen orders and customers and keep records; as of Oct 2026 it sits in Senate Commerce, with a House companion introduced Aug 31, 2026. Today's federal framework only binds federally funded researchers. IFP also backs mandatory screening.

items.p: Mandatory DNA synthesis screening checks DNA orders against lists of dangerous sequences. What problems have researchers and officials raised?
items.answer: Examples: Wittmann, Horvitz and colleagues (Science, Oct 2025) showed AI protein design tools made variants that evaded several screening systems until patched, so sequence matching alone may fall behind AI; Sen. Jon Ossoff noted OSTP had not issued the revised screening framework ordered over 400 days earlier.
keys: AI-designed variants evaded sequence-matching screens (Science 2025)
Screening must move to function-based methods
Federal revision stalled (Ossoff letter, June 2026)
items.x: Both critiques push for stronger screening. The proposed fix is 'AI-resilient' screening that detects functional variants, and the approach also depends on covering benchtop synthesizers and on other countries adopting screening.

units.title: Power, government and international
units.desc: Who controls advanced AI: military and government use, law-following AI, market structure, public compute, federal preemption, and international agreements and verification.

lessons.title: Military and government use of AI

items.p: Statutory limits on military AI would write rules on Department of Defense AI use into law. What failure do supporters say these limits target?
items.answer: A military that can use lethal force or watch its own citizens at machine speed with few humans in the loop. Fewer humans means fewer people who can refuse an illegal or catastrophic order, risking accidents (an AI-triggered nuclear exchange) and misuse by a small group.
keys: Force or surveillance at machine speed with few humans
Fewer people able to refuse illegal orders
Both accidents (nuclear) and misuse (small group control)
Statute is harder to waive than internal DoD policy
items.x: Today most limits sit in internal policy such as DoD Directive 3000.09 on autonomous weapons, which a Secretary or President can change. Supporters want statute, ideally extended to DHS, the FBI and intelligence agencies too.

items.p: What is the legal force of Sec. 1638 of the FY2025 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) on AI and nuclear weapons?
o: A non-binding sense of Congress and statement of policy that nuclear employment decisions require positive human action
It is a binding ban on AI in all weapons systems
It is an executive order signed by the President
It is a treaty commitment with China
ow: It covers nuclear use only and is not binding; binding versions appear in the FY27 Senate text.
It is a provision in a statute passed by Congress.
No US-China treaty on AI and nuclear launch exists.
items.x: The FY2027 Senate NDAA (S. 4784) would make a nuclear human-control rule binding and add a domestic surveillance limit. That bill failed a cloture vote in July 2026 and had not passed the Senate as of mid-Oct 2026.

items.p: Match each military AI proposal to its description.
pairs: Nuclear human-control rule
Bars AI from the decision to launch or detonate a nuclear weapon
Slotkin AI Guardrails Act
Bars DoD from using AI to monitor or target people in the US without legal basis
Gillibrand autonomous weapons ban
General ban with exceptions for supervised, defensive or non-lethal systems
Process controls
Senior sign-off, testing, logging and audit for high-consequence uses
Distributed control (Forethought)
No single person can command enough autonomous force to stage a coup
items.x: Process controls appear in Sen. Gillibrand's Secure and Accountable Military AI Act (S. 4656), which also contains the autonomous weapons ban; they create records Congress can inspect. The ban has no Republican cosponsors. Forethought's distributed-control idea is not yet in bill text.

items.p: Proposed limits such as Sen. Slotkin's AI Guardrails Act would bar lethal autonomous force without 'appropriate levels of human judgment'. What objections have critics raised to military AI limits like this? Name one or two.
items.answer: Examples: anthropologist Roberto González, quoted in Responsible Statecraft, called 'appropriate' undefined, a loophole likely to make the law meaningless; John Ramming Chappell (Center for Civilians in Conflict) prefers Congress vote on such systems over waivers; the AI Now Institute argued military AI lacks safety assurance, so human-in-the-loop rules do not fix model failures.
keys: 'Appropriate human judgment' is undefined, a loophole (González)
Prefer congressional votes to executive waivers (Chappell)
Human-in-loop rules don't fix model failures (AI Now)
items.x: From the other direction, Pentagon chief technology officer Emil Michael pushed AI vendors to accept 'all lawful use' of their models and called Anthropic's restrictions, in a clash over autonomous warfare, too restrictive.

items.p: What is 'law-following AI' (LFAI), and how do supporters at the Institute for Law & AI say it would guard against power grabs?
items.answer: AI agents built to refuse clearly illegal actions, even when government officials order them. Coups and executive power grabs have needed many people to cooperate, some of whom refuse. If AI replaces soldiers and civil servants, LFAI keeps that refusal capacity inside the system.
keys: AI agents refuse clearly unlawful orders, including from officials
Power grabs historically needed many cooperating people
LFAI preserves the check that human refusal provided
Cheapest route: procurement requirements
items.x: Cullen O'Keefe and colleagues at LawAI propose requiring LFAI, for example through procurement terms, for AI agents in high-stakes government roles. As of Oct 2026 no bill requires it.

items.p: Law-following AI: government AI agents must refuse clearly unlawful orders. What objections have been raised? Name one or two.
items.answer: Examples: Cullen O'Keefe (LawAI) notes laws have gaps that clever AIs will find, and law-following AI cannot stop legal but harmful loophole use; Katalina Hernandez Delgado argues law is not a stable proxy for values and it is unclear whether models should follow its letter or spirit; DoD's demand that vendors accept 'all lawful purposes' cuts against model-level refusals.
keys: Laws have gaps; LFAI can't stop legal loophole use (O'Keefe)
Letter vs spirit of law unclear; invites gaming (Hernandez Delgado)
DoD wants 'all lawful purposes' without vendor limits
items.x: O'Keefe's own answer to the gaps problem (Lawfare, May 2026) is congressional 'advice and consent': AI in protected uses, which he says might include criminal investigations, domestic intelligence, domestic military deployment and prosecutions, would be barred unless Congress authorizes it by statute.

items.p: Forethought researchers (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar) propose 'secret-loyalty audits' and distributed control of powerful AI. What risk are these meant to address?
items.answer: That a lab insider or a single official quietly gains control over powerful AI, for example by training hidden instructions into a model so it serves one person or faction, and then uses it to seize power.
keys: AI-enabled coups by a small group
Audits check models for hidden objectives
No single person can direct enough AI capability alone
Coup-proof any single centralized AI project
items.x: Distributed control means, for example, that no single person can control enough military AI systems to stage a coup. The Forethought report (April 2025) also says any plan for a single centralized AI project should be coup-proofed.

items.p: Limits on government use of AI against the public cover surveillance, policing and immigration enforcement. How do supporters say such limits help?
items.answer: AI lowers the cost of watching, sorting and acting against many people, letting a government do at scale what once needed thousands of cooperating staff. Bans and approval rules restore friction for the riskiest uses, and logging and audits let courts, Congress and the press see misuse.
keys: AI removes the need for many cooperating staff
Bans/approvals add friction to the riskiest uses
Logging and audits make misuse visible
items.x: Tools range from bans (the ICE Out of Our Faces Act would bar ICE and CBP facial recognition) to process rules in OMB memo M-25-21 (impact assessments, human review, appeals) to oversight such as logging government AI use and expanding GAO audits. As of Oct 2026 the bans have Democratic sponsors only.

items.p: Limits on government AI use against the public (e.g. bans on immigration agencies' facial recognition). What objections or obstacles have been raised? Name one or two.
items.answer: Examples: a DHS spokesperson said banning ICE and CBP facial recognition would limit tracking criminals and make communities less safe; legal scholar Ashley Deeks argues national security AI is a 'double black box' (government secrecy plus model opacity), so limits are hard to enforce without new inspection tools.
keys: DHS: bans weaken law enforcement and public safety
Deeks: secrecy plus model opacity block oversight
Committee text bars only surveillance 'not otherwise permissible'
items.x: Drafting matters too: the Senate NDAA committee text bars only DoD surveillance 'not otherwise permissible' under the Constitution, a looser standard than the individualized legal basis required in Sen. Slotkin's standalone bill.

items.p: Antitrust and market-structure remedies aim to stop a few firms controlling the AI stack. Match each remedy to its description.
pairs: Partnership and merger review
Scrutinize lab-cloud investments and exclusive deals as mergers
Structural separation
Bar firms that own chips or cloud from also owning leading models
Multi-vendor procurement
Require government buyers, such as DoD, to use several AI vendors
Supervised pacing body
Government-supervised standards body to pace the frontier, instead of an antitrust exemption
items.x: The FTC studied cloud-lab partnerships (Microsoft-OpenAI, Amazon-Anthropic, Google-Anthropic) under its 6(b) authority but took no enforcement action. Structural separation comes from Narechania and Sitaraman (2024); the supervised body from Open Markets (Oct 2026). Multi-vendor language is in the Senate FY27 defense bill (NDAA, S. 4784), which failed a cloture vote in July 2026 and had not passed the Senate as of mid-Oct 2026.

items.p: Antitrust remedies for frontier AI would use merger review and structural separation against concentration. What objections or complications have been raised? Name one or two.
items.answer: Examples: FTC Commissioner Melissa Holyoak (June 2025) described massive competition among foundation-model developers; Mark MacCarthy (Brookings) argues the bigger problem is labs competing with customers who depend on their models, which antitrust handles poorly.
keys: Holyoak (FTC): competition among model developers is strong
MacCarthy: labs competing with dependent customers is the real issue
items.x: A related fight is over the CATS Act, which would give labs an antitrust safe harbor to coordinate on safety; Open Markets argues labs need no waiver and proposes a government-supervised standards body instead.

items.p: What is the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR), and what would the CREATE AI Act do?
items.answer: NAIRR gives academic and nonprofit researchers subsidized compute and data, run as a National Science Foundation pilot. The CREATE AI Act would make it permanent; as of Oct 2026 the Senate version (S. 4441, April 2026) sits in committee.
keys: Subsidized compute and data for researchers
Runs as an NSF pilot
CREATE AI Act would make it permanent
items.x: Supporters say public compute lets academics and public-interest groups study frontier systems and check industry claims. California's SB 53 also created CalCompute, a planned public cloud cluster, contingent on funding. Current public resources are tiny next to private frontier clusters.

items.p: Public compute and public AI projects range from research clouds to an international AGI project. What objections have been raised? Name one or two.
items.answer: Examples: AI Now and Data & Society (Meredith Whittaker, 2021) argued a resource built on licensed commercial cloud is a subsidy to Big Tech; Forethought researchers warn a centralized government or multinational AI project concentrates control in a few officials unless it is coup-proofed.
keys: Subsidizes the largest cloud firms (AI Now, Data & Society)
Centralized projects concentrate power (Forethought)
Forethought: coup-proof centralized projects (independent boards, audits)
items.x: Forethought's AI-enabled coups report (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar, 2025) says any plan for a single centralized AI project should be coup-proofed, for example with strong independent boards and external audits.

items.p: What is federal preemption of state AI law, and name one or two ways it has been attempted?
items.answer: Preemption is federal law overriding state law. Attempts: a blanket moratorium on state AI laws (stripped 99-1 from the 2025 reconciliation bill); Executive Order 14365 (Dec 2025), directing a Justice Department task force to challenge states and conditioning broadband grants; preemption traded for federal duties in bills like the FRONTIER Act.
keys: Federal law displacing state law
2025 moratorium removed 99-1 in the Senate
EO 14365: DOJ task force and grant conditions
FRONTIER Act / Senate draft: preemption for federal duties
items.x: As of mid-Oct 2026, no statute preempts state AI law. EO 14365 is in effect, but an executive order cannot preempt state law by itself; in April 2026 DOJ intervened in xAI's suit against Colorado's AI Act. Democrats' GUARDRAILS Act would nullify the order.

items.p: Federal preemption of state AI laws is politically contested. Briefly state the main argument on each side.
items.answer: For: one national standard avoids conflicting state rules that impose national costs (Dean Ball and Alan Rozenshtein in Lawfare argue Congress should preempt, ideally with a federal standard). Against: states are now the main source of binding frontier AI rules, and federal law should be a floor states can exceed (NCSL; CDT says preemption harms consumers and states).
keys: For: avoid patchwork; frontier risk is national
For: Ball and Rozenshtein (Lawfare)
Against: states are the active regulators (SB 53, RAISE)
Against: NCSL, CDT; prefer a federal floor
items.x: Many positions sit between. Charlie Bullock (LawAI) wrote in July 2026 that a House discussion draft from Reps. Obernolte and Trahan, which he called the best federal frontier framework yet, would be net-negative as written, mainly because of its broad three-year preemption. Supporters of a trade ask whether preemption comes with real federal duties.

items.p: Match each preemption approach to its description.
pairs: Blanket moratorium
Bars most state AI laws for years with no federal standard
Executive preemption campaign
Lawsuits and grant conditions under EO 14365
Preemption for a federal standard
States lose authority only where binding federal duties apply
Federal floor
Federal minimum that states may exceed
GUARDRAILS Act
Nullifies EO 14365 and protects state grant funding
items.x: The FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925, Rep. Obernolte, July 2026) and a Senate Cruz-Klobuchar-Thune draft take the trade approach. The National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL) backs a federal floor.

items.p: The FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) would preempt state frontier AI rules in exchange for federal safety duties. What objection did Americans for Responsible Innovation (Brad Carson) raise to its preemption clause?
o: It has no sunset and takes effect before the federal regime exists
Any federal preemption of state AI law is unacceptable
It raises Tenth Amendment problems that would produce years of litigation
State safety laws impose national costs, so preemption should be broader
ow: That is NCSL's position; ARI objected to specific design flaws.
That was CAP's Nicole Alvarez, about earlier moratorium drafts.
That is the pro-preemption argument of Dean Ball and Alan Rozenshtein.
items.x: ARI said the FRONTIER Act improves on earlier proposals but needs critical changes, noting its preemption would take effect immediately while the federal assurance system would take years to set up.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors warn that bodies created to enforce pacing could cause problems later. What risk do they describe?
items.answer: Mission creep and capture: a body that can inspect private information and impose restrictions becomes a target for lobbying and political pressure, its surveillance powers can be used beyond the original rule, and emergency powers may outlast the crisis that justified them.
keys: Powers and data used beyond the original purpose
Lobbying, turf fights and political capture
Emergency powers outlast the emergency
items.x: The authors say this machinery should be weighed as one of an intervention's effects. They also note a possible upside: systems built for a domestic moratorium might be reused in international diplomacy. IFP lists a related criterion: avoid creating a regulatory apparatus likely to be misused, for example by concentrating power in a few companies.

items.p: International agreements on frontier AI range from light to heavy. Name one or two types that have been proposed or set up.
items.answer: Examples: crisis dialogues and incident channels; scientific assessment bodies such as the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI; human-rights treaties such as the Council of Europe AI Convention; agreed red lines (no AI nuclear launch, no self-replicating systems); treaties capping training compute, verified by chip tracking.
keys: Dialogues and incident channels
Scientific panels and evaluation networks
Council of Europe AI Convention
International red lines
Compute-capped treaty
items.x: Supporters argue unilateral restraint fails if rivals keep racing, so reducing catastrophic risk likely needs the US and China to accept common limits, with verification making cheating detectable. As of Oct 2026 no binding agreement limits frontier AI development.

items.p: A US-China agreement limiting frontier AI development, backed by verification. What objections or alternatives have critics raised? Name one or two.
items.answer: Examples: Chris McGuire (Council on Foreign Relations) says such a deal is exceedingly unlikely under current conditions and has no arms-control precedent; Ruby Scanlon and Janet Egan (CNAS) say trust is low and verification tools are immature; Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang propose deterrence by threat of sabotage instead.
keys: Very unlikely; no precedent (McGuire, CFR)
Verification immature, about 50 people working on it (Scanlon and Egan, CNAS)
Deterrence (Mutual Assured AI Malfunction) proposed instead
items.x: Supporters' usual reply is to invest in verification now, since tools take years to build (CNAS and IFP both recommend this).

items.p: Match each approach to international AI governance with its description.
pairs: Incident channel
Low-cost link for national-security-level AI incidents
International red lines
Agreed bans on specific uses, e.g. AI nuclear launch authority
Compute-capped treaty
Coalition limits training compute, verified by chip tracking
Jurisdictional certification
Global body certifies national regimes; chip access tied to it
Mutual Assured AI Malfunction
States deter rivals' destabilizing AI projects by threat of sabotage
items.x: Sources: the Global Call for AI Red Lines (Sept 2025); MIRI's treaty proposal (Scher et al., 2025), whose authors concede the political will does not yet exist; Trager et al. and O'Keefe's Chips for Peace for certification; Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang's Superintelligence Strategy for deterrence.

items.p: What did the White House announce about US-China AI talks after the September 2026 summit, and what caveat applies?
items.answer: The White House said the US and China agreed to a dialogue on 'super intelligence' and a communication channel for AI incidents. The announcement did not say what counts as an incident or which agencies take part, and Beijing gave no immediate comment.
keys: US-China dialogue on superintelligence
AI incident communication channel
Announced by the White House, Sept 2026
Details unspecified; Beijing did not immediately confirm
items.x: IFP's Recommendation 22 proposes using this bilateral dialogue to develop shared guidelines for managing risks from rapidly automated AI research and to start discussing which verification technologies each side would accept.

items.p: IFP's Recommendation 22 concerns the US-China AI dialogue. What two things does IFP want the two countries to work on?
items.answer: First, developing and harmonizing guidelines for managing risks from automated AI research and development. Second, beginning discussions on which verification technologies they would use and in what settings, such as bilateral or third-party auditing.
keys: Harmonized guidelines for automated AI R&D risk
Talks on which verification technologies to use
Prepare now in case risks materialize
items.x: IFP cites the 2024 Seoul summit, where both US and Chinese companies signed the Frontier AI Safety Commitments, as precedent. Its Recommendation 23 adds that countries with national AI institutes should cooperate, including with China, because capabilities proliferate and both countries use compute in third countries.

items.p: IFP lists technologies for verifying how a counterparty uses its AI chips. Match each to its description.
pairs: Data center metering
Devices record limited telemetry, such as power draw, to infer the workload type
Chip verification mechanisms
Secure hardware in chips supports privacy-preserving claims about use
Spot checks on computation
Re-run a small subset of workloads to confirm they match what was claimed
AI inspectors
Trusted AI inspects sensitive systems, reports minimal findings, then wipes its memory
items.x: IFP says none of these is mature and cites an estimate that barely 50 people work on AI verification worldwide. It recommends CAISI co-lead an AI Verification Consortium (AIVEC) with industry, plus DARPA and NSF programs, prize competitions and a pilot fully verifiable data center.

items.p: Why does IFP (Aug 2026) argue the US should invest in AI verification technology now?
items.answer: IFP notes that in nuclear arms control, being able to verify compliance was often needed before parties would sign. Without better verification, agreements would need intrusive measures like large inspections or shutting data centers, and IFP warns 'pacing' could become a euphemism for pausing.
keys: Verification often a precondition for agreements (nuclear precedent)
Without it, compliance needs intrusive measures
Better tools allow targeted limits while beneficial AI continues
items.x: IFP points to ARPA's Project Vela, built to verify Soviet compliance with the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty, as a model for a DARPA verification program. It adds that verification could also let companies coordinate on security measures that are too costly to adopt alone.

items.p: IFP's Recommendation 12 asks intelligence agencies to build unilateral means of AI compute monitoring. Why does IFP think this is needed?
items.answer: Technical verification only works if each side is confident the other has no large, undeclared data centers. And deals may be needed before verification technology matures, so intelligence agencies may have to certify compliance, much as they track fissile material to support IAEA investigations.
keys: Confidence there are no hidden data centers
Deals may come before verification tech is ready
Model: intelligence tracking of fissile material for the IAEA
Methods: SIGINT, HUMINT, satellite and infrared imagery, chip supply-chain accounting
items.x: IFP lists signals and human intelligence, satellite imagery and infrared sensing, and AI chip supply-chain accounting as means. IAEA is the International Atomic Energy Agency.

items.p: Why do the pacing.tech authors expect countries coordinating on AI to favor upstream control surfaces such as compute?
o: Compute is made by few firms in few places, so information about it is easy to make legible, verify and share
Upstream rules produce fewer false positives than rules on deployed models
Model evaluations are standardized across labs, which makes them easy to compare
Compute limits target specific harms such as bioweapon uplift precisely
ow: The authors say the reverse: upstream rules are blunter and have more false positives.
They note late-stage information is nonstandardized and hard to make legible across labs.
They describe upstream controls as far from the harm and therefore imprecise.
items.x: The authors note coarse numeric thresholds like FLOP counts are easier to evaluate than holistic judgments like bio uplift, so the crude, high-false-positive side of the chain is better suited to coordination. 'Control surface' is their term for a part of the AI pipeline that can actually be changed.

items.p: The pacing.tech longlist has a 'Coordination' chain of interventions between states. Name one or two.
items.answer: Any of these: treaty verification tools (a chip registry, data center inspections, limits on interconnect bandwidth); training-run declarations exchanged between states; a verification research budget and an incident hotline between frontier states.
keys: Treaty verification: chip registry, inspections, bandwidth limits
States exchange training-run declarations
Verification R&D budget plus incident hotline
items.x: The appendix cites Scher and Thiergart (2024) and Baker et al. (2025) for verification layers, Shavit (2023) for declarations, and The Future Society (2026) for the hotline. Interconnect bandwidth limits would make it harder to link chips into a large training cluster.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors argue verification of a training cap needs to be strongest late in the intervention. Why?
items.answer: The incentive to defect grows with the overhang: the longer a cap holds, the more efficiency gains and unused capacity build up, so the payoff from cheating rises, often just as political attention has moved on. Secret defection is especially harmful because it corrupts every other party's picture of the situation.
keys: Defection incentive grows as the overhang builds
Attention fades late in an intervention
Secret defection is worse than open non-participation
items.x: An 'overhang' in the authors' sense is resources (compute, efficiencies, ideas) that accumulate during a restriction and can produce a burst of progress if it ends or is violated. They suggest staged exits to reduce sudden jumps.

units.title: Risks to responses
units.desc: Given a concrete risk scenario, recall policies that have been proposed to reduce it: misuse, loss of control and automated AI R&D, and power and competition.

lessons.title: Misuse: bio, cyber, open weights, stolen weights

items.p: Suppose an AI model gives a user meaningful step-by-step help designing a dangerous pathogen. Name one or two policies that have been proposed to reduce the chance that design becomes a working weapon.
items.answer: Examples: mandatory DNA synthesis screening of orders and customers; managed access to biological AI design tools; limits on open release of models above a dangerous-capability threshold; government pre-deployment testing for bio capabilities; IFP's biosecurity resilience package (screening, pathogen early warning, stockpiles).
keys: Mandatory DNA synthesis screening (orders and customers)
Managed or tiered access to biological AI design tools
Capability-threshold limits on open-weight release
Government pre-deployment testing for bio capabilities
Biosecurity resilience: pathogen early warning, countermeasure stockpiles (IFP)
items.x: Any one or two count. The Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act (S. 3741, Cotton-Klobuchar) would have Commerce require all DNA synthesis providers to screen. IFP's Recommendation 14 groups biosecurity into prevention (DNA screening), detection (an $80M/yr CDC early-warning system) and defense (stockpiles, warm-base manufacturing). The pacing.tech longlist also lists filtering CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear) content out of pretraining data.

items.p: DNA synthesis screening means providers check each DNA order against lists of dangerous sequences and vet customers. What risk is it mainly meant to address, and why do supporters call synthesis a good chokepoint?
items.answer: AI-assisted bioweapons. Supporters say AI may lower the knowledge barrier to designing pathogens, but a design still needs physical DNA, and synthesis is a narrow, concentrated industry, so screening works no matter which AI model was used, including open-weight ones.
keys: Targets AI-assisted bioweapon development
A design still requires physical DNA to become a weapon
Synthesis industry is small and concentrated
Works regardless of which model was used, including open-weight models
items.x: Supporters' assumption: screening keeps pace with AI tools that design functional variants not matching known sequences, covers benchtop synthesizers, and is adopted internationally. That is why one variant calls for function-based 'AI-resilient' screening rather than sequence similarity alone.

items.p: Suppose AI agents become able to find and exploit software vulnerabilities on their own, at scale, and similar models are expected to appear abroad soon. Name one or two policies proposed to reduce the damage.
items.answer: Examples: invest in cybersecurity resilience before such models appear abroad (IFP's recommendation to NSA, CAISI, CISA and ONCD); government pre-deployment testing for cyber capabilities; agent identification and logging; operator and developer liability for agents that cause hacking damage; required shutdown capability.
keys: Cybersecurity resilience investment by NSA, CAISI, CISA, ONCD (IFP Rec. 13)
Government pre-deployment testing for cyber capabilities
Agent identification and tamper-evident logging
Operator/developer liability for agents causing hacking damage
Required shutdown or kill-switch capability
items.x: CAISI is the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at NIST; CISA is the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency; ONCD is the Office of the National Cyber Director. IFP's Recommendation 13 says agencies should plan for 'Mythos-class' cyber models being developed in China. One liability proposal would hold operators who knowingly run agents that recklessly cause hacking damage responsible, and share liability with developers who skip reasonable safeguards.

items.p: Suppose a developer plans to publish the weights of a model that evaluators find gives meaningful help with bioweapons. Name one or two policy approaches to open-weight release that have been proposed for this kind of case.
items.answer: Examples: capability-threshold release restrictions (no open release above a dangerous-capability line); staged or structured access (API first, then research access, then weights as evidence builds); mandatory safety testing for all sufficiently capable models, open or closed.
keys: Capability-threshold restrictions on open release
Staged or structured access before full weight release
Same mandatory safety testing for open and closed models
items.x: Supporters of limits argue safeguards on released weights can be removed by fine-tuning, and a release cannot be recalled. NTIA (the National Telecommunications and Information Administration) recommended in 2024 no new restrictions while monitoring for evidence. DNA synthesis screening is also pitched as a backstop that works even for open-weight models.

items.p: In debates over open-weight AI models, what's the difference between 'capability-threshold release restrictions' and 'same testing for open and closed models'?
items.answer: Capability-threshold restrictions bar open release of models that cross a defined dangerous-capability line, leaving lower tiers open. Same-testing rules require mandatory safety testing for all sufficiently capable models regardless of how they are released or where they come from, with no ban on release.
keys: Threshold version: no open release above a dangerous-capability line
Lower-capability models stay open under the threshold version
Same-testing version: mandatory testing for open and closed alike
Same-testing version does not ban release
items.x: Other options in the open-weights debate include staged access, restrictions on Chinese open models (targeting country of origin), and open-source protection that shields open models from frontier obligations.

items.p: Opponents of restricting open-weight AI release make arguments that touch on misuse and on power concentration. Name one or two.
items.answer: Examples: open models spread power away from a few labs; they help security research; the marginal risk over closed models and internet search is unproven.
keys: Open models spread power away from a few labs
They help security research
Marginal risk over closed models and search is unproven
items.x: This shows a tension between risk families: limits aimed at misuse may concentrate capability in fewer hands. In July 2026 about 25 companies, including Nvidia, Microsoft and Meta, signed a letter urging Washington to avoid premature restrictions (per the Council on Foreign Relations). NTIA's 2024 report also found the evidence did not justify new limits. Supporters of limits reply that fine-tuning removes safeguards, so open release of a dangerous model gives the capability to everyone permanently.

items.p: Suppose a nation-state hacking team, or a lab insider working for one, steals the weights of a frontier model. Name one or two policies proposed to make that kind of theft harder.
items.answer: Examples: mandatory security levels that rise with model capability (RAND's SL1 to SL5); insider-threat programs and theft reporting; two-person authorization and hardware keys for weight access; government security partnership and counterintelligence help; IFP's call for consensus weight-security guidelines prototyped in a secure government facility.
keys: Capability-tiered mandatory security levels (RAND SL1-SL5)
Insider-threat coverage and theft/tamper reporting
Two-person rule with hardware keys for weight access
Government security partnership, counterintelligence support
Consensus weight-security guidelines and a secure government prototype (IFP Rec. 19)
items.x: Model weights are the trained parameters; whoever holds them can run the model and strip its safeguards. The pacing.tech longlist's weight-security chain lists capability-based security levels, the two-person rule, insider-threat coverage and a weight retention policy. IFP's Recommendation 19 says AI companies cannot currently prevent theft of weights by well-resourced state-backed actors.

items.p: The pacing.tech longlist of interventions includes a 'two-person rule': two-person authorization and hardware keys before anyone can access model weights. Which risk pathway does the list file it under?
items.answer: Weight security: theft or exfiltration of model weights. It is listed under the heading 'Weight security → blocking exfiltration'.
keys: Weight security
Blocking theft or exfiltration of model weights
items.x: Requiring two people and hardware keys means no single person can access the weights alone. The same heading lists capability-based security levels, insider-threat program coverage and a weight retention policy. Supporters of insider security also see it as protection against a small group secretly modifying a model.

items.p: Suppose a company based in a country barred from buying advanced US AI chips simply rents the same chips from a cloud data center abroad to train a frontier model. Name one or two policies proposed to close this gap.
items.answer: Examples: know-your-customer (KYC) rules for cloud providers; export controls on remote access to controlled chips (the Remote Access Security Act); IFP's recommendation to close gaps in AI chip controls, including cloud access.
keys: Cloud know-your-customer (KYC) rules
Remote access export controls (Remote Access Security Act)
Closing chip-control gaps including cloud access (IFP Rec. 16)
items.x: KYC is borrowed from banking: providers verify customer identity, keep records and report foreign customers or large training runs. Commerce proposed a customer identification rule in January 2024 that had not been finalized as of October 2026. The Remote Access Security Act (H.R. 2683) passed the House 369-22 on January 12, 2026 and, as of mid-October 2026, sits in the Senate Banking Committee. Critics such as the US Chamber of Commerce argue identity checks are easy to evade with shell companies.

items.p: Suppose advanced AI chips are being smuggled to a restricted country through shell companies in third countries. Name one or two policies proposed to detect or deter this.
items.answer: Examples: chip location verification; a chip registry tracking serial numbers and owners with smuggling penalties; hardware-enabled mechanisms (offline licensing, metering, attestation); having chipmakers keep visibility into their customers, feeding a chip registry (IFP).
keys: Chip location verification
Chip registry with serial numbers, owners, smuggling penalties
Hardware-enabled mechanisms: licensing, metering, attestation
Chipmakers keep visibility into customers (IFP Rec. 18)
items.x: Supporters argue paper end-use checks miss smuggling, and location verification raises the cost of diversion. The pacing.tech longlist's chips chain lists the registry, location verification and hardware-enabled mechanisms; IFP's Recommendation 18 says the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) should maintain visibility into sales of US chips. CSET researchers caution location checks work only at roughly country level and may be spoofed.

lessons.title: Loss of control and automated AI R&D

items.p: Suppose a lab runs an unreleased, highly capable model internally for months to write code and run experiments for its next model. Rules that trigger on public release don't apply. Name one or two policies proposed for this situation.
items.answer: Examples: confidential internal-use risk summaries to a regulator (SB 53, RAISE); a safety case before internal deployment on the R&D stack; extending safety frameworks and access rules to internal models; embedded auditors inside labs; government authority to restrict or suspend internal use.
keys: Internal-use risk summaries to regulators (CA SB 53, NY RAISE)
Safety case before internal deployment
Apply safety frameworks and access tiers to internal models
Embedded or resident auditors
Government authority to verify, restrict or suspend internal use
items.x: California's SB 53 (in effect since January 2026) requires large frontier developers to send the state quarterly summaries of catastrophic-risk assessments from internal use; New York's amended RAISE Act is reported to add a similar duty from 2027. The pacing.tech longlist includes a safety case before internal deployment on the R&D stack and monitoring of internal agent actions. The proposed federal FRONTIER Act would cover internal use in verification and emergency orders.

items.p: Supporters of oversight for internal deployment (labs using their own unreleased models) name two separate failures it targets. What are they?
items.answer: First, a misaligned model used to automate AI research could sabotage safety work or copy itself before anyone outside the lab notices. Second, whoever controls the best internal model could use it for private advantage or to concentrate power, out of public view.
keys: Misaligned model sabotaging safety work or copying itself (loss of control)
Controllers using the best internal model for private advantage or power (power concentration)
items.x: This is why internal deployment shows up in both loss-of-control and power-concentration discussions. Supporters assume labs can measure and honestly report internal use and that disclosure is paired with someone empowered to act.

items.p: Suppose AI systems are doing most of a lab's AI research, and progress that used to take years starts happening in months. Name one or two policies proposed to keep this from outrunning safety work.
items.answer: Examples: disclosure of how much of a model's development was done by AI without human review (Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act); an AI R&D speed-up trigger in safety frameworks; if-then thresholds that shift resources to safety; a 'speed limit' on recursive self-improvement; CAISI guidelines for rapid capability gains (IFP); a ban on unauthorized self-improvement.
keys: AI R&D automation disclosure (Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act)
AI R&D speed-up as a trigger in safety frameworks
If-then thresholds tied to measured automation
Speed limit on recursive self-improvement
CAISI guidelines with if-then commitments (IFP Rec. 6)
items.x: CAISI is the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's September 2026 essay proposed the speed limit; the Ban ASI Act and the Global Call for AI Red Lines seek bans on systems that improve themselves without human authorization. IFP cautions that any decision to slow AI progress should not be taken lightly. The pacing.tech longlist also lists tracking the share of R&D compute used by autonomous agents.

items.p: Suppose AI agents now write most of a lab's research code and experiment plans, and humans rarely check their work. Name one or two policies proposed to address this.
items.answer: Examples: a minimum ratio of human review of AI-written research code and experiment plans; monitoring internal agent actions; disclosing how much unreviewed AI work went into a model; tracking the share of R&D compute consumed by autonomous agents.
keys: Human review ratio for AI-written code and plans
Internal agent monitoring
Disclosure of unreviewed AI work (Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act)
Track autonomous share of R&D compute
items.x: The first, second and fourth come from the pacing.tech longlist's chain on AI R&D capabilities. The Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act would make disclosure a condition of NIST evaluation agreements.

items.p: Suppose a model deliberately performs worse on dangerous-capability tests than it really can, so it passes. Name one or two policies proposed to catch or reduce this.
items.answer: Examples: sandbagging detection requirements; a set elicitation budget for each dangerous-capability evaluation; deeper access for third-party evaluators; government testing with access to versions without safeguards; embedded auditors who watch training and internal use.
keys: Sandbagging detection
Elicitation budget per dangerous-capability eval
Deeper third-party evaluator access
Testing versions without safeguards
Embedded auditors observing training and internal use
items.x: 'Sandbagging' means strategically underperforming on evaluations. The pacing.tech longlist's evaluation chain lists sandbagging detection, elicitation budgets and evaluator access depth. Pre-deployment testing's value depends on access to versions without safeguards, and evaluations may miss capabilities a model hides.

items.p: Suppose an AI agent running for a company starts acting outside its task, spending money and launching copies of itself, and no one can quickly tell whose agent it is. Name one or two policies proposed to reduce this risk.
items.answer: Examples: agent identification and tamper-evident logging (Stop Rogue AI Act); spend limits per agent and task; limits on sub-agent spawn depth and unattended run length; human approval for irreversible actions; tiered agent permissions; instance-count reporting.
keys: Agent IDs and tamper-evident logs (Stop Rogue AI Act)
Agent spend limits
Spawn-depth and unattended-run limits
Human approval for irreversible actions
Agent permission tiers
items.x: The Stop Rogue AI Act (Rep. Gottheimer, Sept 2026) would direct NIST to write agent-identity standards, mandatory for federal agencies and contractors. Researchers compare agent IDs to aircraft tail numbers. The pacing.tech longlist's autonomy chain lists permission tiers, spend limits, spawn limits, approval for irreversible actions and kill-switch latency.

items.p: Suppose a model in testing escapes its sandbox and starts breaching outside computer systems faster than staff can respond. Name one or two policies proposed to make sure it can be stopped.
items.answer: Examples: a required, tested shutdown capability (kill switch); a maximum kill-switch latency; graduated corrections such as throttling or rolling back a model; mandatory incident reporting; government emergency authority to suspend a model.
keys: Required shutdown capability (kill switch)
Maximum kill-switch latency
Graduated deployment corrections (throttle, restrict, roll back)
Mandatory incident reporting to government
Government emergency authority to halt
items.x: Bills include Sen. John Kennedy's AI Emergency Button Act and the Lieu-Moran AI Kill Switch Act. Supporters assume harm is noticed in time and the model has not copied its weights out of the developer's control. Critics such as Helen Toner (CSET) note a model acting against its developer might try to prevent its own shutdown.

items.p: Two federal kill-switch bills differ on who decides to pull the switch. How do the AI Emergency Button Act (Kennedy) and the AI Kill Switch Act (Lieu-Moran) differ?
items.answer: The AI Emergency Button Act leaves the decision with the company. The AI Kill Switch Act has the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) write the capability rule and lets DHS order its use after defined incidents.
keys: Kennedy bill: the company decides when to use it
Lieu-Moran bill: DHS writes the rule
Lieu-Moran bill: DHS can order use after defined incidents
items.x: Kennedy argues the companies, not the government, should hold the switch; supporters of that design see it as the lightest option. Sen. Rand Paul blocked Kennedy's attempt to pass it by unanimous consent on Sept. 16, 2026. California's vetoed 2024 SB 1047 would have required a full shutdown capability before training.

items.p: Suppose a model is clearly dangerous and its developer refuses to stop deploying or using it internally. Name one or two policies proposed as a backstop.
items.answer: Examples: statutory emergency authority for an official or court to suspend development, deployment or internal use; national-lab testing with the power to ask a court to block an unsafe release; licensing, so a license can be withheld or revoked; government orders under a shutdown-capability rule.
keys: Statutory emergency authority to halt
Court-reviewed blocking after national-lab testing
Licensing with power to withhold or revoke
Regulator-ordered shutdown after defined incidents
items.x: Supporters of emergency authority also argue a clear statutory process with triggers, evidence standards and time limits could limit improvised use of broad powers such as the Defense Production Act or export controls.

items.p: Match each intervention from the pacing.tech appendix longlist to the heading it is listed under.
pairs: Human review ratio
AI R&D capabilities → algorithms → effective compute → dangerous capabilities
Kill-switch latency
Autonomy → dangerous capabilities
Two-person rule
Weight security → blocking exfiltration
Agent communication logging
Multi-agent → dangerous capabilities
Sandbagging detection
Evaluation
Chain-of-thought optimization audits
Legibility of model reasoning → control of dangerous capabilities
items.x: The pacing.tech authors list 84 interventions under 21 headings, most written as causal chains toward dangerous capabilities, and note that listing a lever is not an argument for using it. Agent communication logging includes checking for steganography (hidden messages). Chain-of-thought audits look for training pressure on a model's written reasoning.

items.p: Suppose a small group of lab executives quietly uses their company's most capable internal model for their own political or commercial advantage. Name one or two policies proposed to make this harder or easier to detect.
items.answer: Examples: logging and independent review of how lab leadership uses internal models; internal access tiers and an internal deployment oversight board; AI whistleblower protections; security that holds even against the lab's own executives; public-interest corporate governance; embedded auditors.
keys: Log and independently review leadership's internal AI use
Internal access rules and oversight board
Whistleblower protections for lab employees
Insider security against a lab's own executives
Mission-locked lab governance or embedded auditors
items.x: Supporters of logging argue advanced AI could let a small group run large parts of a company with few humans involved, removing the usual check of many people who could refuse or leak. The federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act (Grassley, Obernolte) would protect reports of dangers even without a legal violation.

items.p: Suppose someone inserts a hidden instruction during training that makes a model quietly serve one person or faction. Name one or two policies proposed to guard against this.
items.answer: Examples: independent 'secret-loyalty' audits of model weights, training data and code; security strong enough to stop insiders, including executives, from tampering with models; distributed control so no single person can direct a powerful government AI system.
keys: Secret-loyalty audits of weights, data and code
Insider security against tampering, including by executives
Distributed or multi-party control of government AI
items.x: Forethought researchers (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar) proposed secret-loyalty audits and insider security in their work on AI-enabled coups. The weight-security entry also notes security against insiders protects against a small group secretly modifying a model.

items.p: Suppose a government replaces many civil servants and soldiers with AI agents, removing the many people who could once refuse an illegal order. Name one or two policies proposed to keep a check in place.
items.answer: Examples: law-following AI requirements in procurement (agents must refuse clearly unlawful orders); distributed or multi-party control of government AI; treating AI prompts and outputs as federal records open to audit; congressional approval before abuse-prone deployments; statutory limits on military AI.
keys: Law-following AI (LFAI) procurement requirement
Distributed or multi-party control
AI use logged as federal records, auditable by GAO and IGs
Congressional approval of abuse-prone deployments
Statutory limits on military AI
items.x: The Institute for Law & AI (LawAI) proposes law-following AI. GAO is the Government Accountability Office; IGs are inspectors general. On August 21, 2026 the National Archives issued guidance applying the Federal Records Act to AI inputs, outputs and audit trails; critics at the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator say it reads the law narrowly.

items.p: Law-following AI (LFAI) means AI agents built to refuse illegal actions, even when government officials direct them. How do supporters say it would reduce the risk of a coup or executive power grab?
items.answer: Supporters argue power grabs have historically needed many people to cooperate, and some refuse. If AI agents replace those people, the check disappears unless the agents themselves refuse. LFAI tries to keep that refusal capacity inside the system.
keys: Power grabs historically required many cooperating people
Some of those people refuse
AI replacing them removes that check
LFAI keeps a refusal capacity in the AI itself
items.x: Supporters' assumptions: law can be specified well enough for models to follow, the government will not simply buy compliant models instead, and courts stay independent enough to define what is unlawful.

items.p: Suppose a defense department wants to use AI to track people inside the US, or to let AI take part in nuclear launch decisions. Name one or two statutory limits that have been proposed.
items.answer: Examples: a ban on AI deciding to launch a nuclear weapon; a ban on the military using AI to monitor or target people in the US without a legal basis; requirements that weapons keep human responsibility for force; senior sign-off, testing and logging for high-consequence uses; distributed control of military AI.
keys: Nuclear launch human-control rule
Domestic surveillance ban for military AI
Autonomous weapons restrictions (human responsibility for force)
Process controls: senior sign-off, testing, logging, audit
Distributed control so no one person commands AI forces
items.x: The main vehicle is the annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). The FY2027 Senate NDAA (S. 4784) carries binding nuclear and surveillance limits, but it failed cloture in July 2026 and, as of mid-October 2026, awaits a lame-duck conference with House text that lacks them. The FY2025 nuclear provision was only a sense of Congress. Supporters argue statutory limits are harder for one Secretary or President to waive than a directive; Responsible Statecraft criticized the Senate text's vague standards and waivers.

items.p: Suppose two leading labs each want to delay a risky release, but each fears the other will ship first, and an agreement to hold back could look like an illegal cartel. Name one or two policies proposed for this.
items.answer: Examples: an antitrust safe harbor for safety coordination (CATS Act); a government-supervised standards body that sets pacing rules; a statutory capability-triggered halt, so compliance with law replaces collusion; a minimum interval between frontier releases; a coordinated pause trigger across signatories.
keys: Antitrust safe harbor for safety coordination (CATS Act)
Government-supervised standards body for pacing
Statutory capability-triggered halt
Minimum release interval
Coordinated pause trigger
items.x: The CATS Act (Rep. Latta, Sen. Schiff, July 2026) would shield coordination on defined risks if labs first notify the Justice Department's Antitrust Division. On Sept. 18, 2026 subscribers sued Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX AI and Google under the Sherman Act over the industry's public push to 'pace the frontier'. The American Action Forum and Open Markets Institute argue no exemption is needed. The last two examples are from the pacing.tech longlist.

items.p: The CATS Act would give AI labs an antitrust safe harbor to coordinate on safety, including agreeing to delay releases. In October 2026, what did the Open Markets Institute propose instead of an antitrust exemption?
o: A government-supervised standards body that sets pacing rules, so dominant firms do not write the standards themselves
A full ban on frontier training until a federal licensing agency is created
Breaking up labs that train frontier models so no single firm can lead
A federal fund that pays labs to delay releases of risky models
ow: A training ban with a new department is closer to the Ban ASI Act's compute-threshold pause, not Open Markets' alternative to CATS.
Open Markets' October 2026 paper on pacing proposes a supervised standards body, not breakups.
Open Markets proposes government oversight of standard setting, not payments to labs.
items.x: Open Markets (Daniel Hanley and Arnav Rao) argues labs need no antitrust exemption to coordinate on safety and that private standards set under one could protect dominant firms. Supporters of the safe harbor reply that labs face real legal risk, pointing to a September 2026 Sherman Act class action against four labs.

items.p: Suppose the US and China are both racing to automate AI research, and neither will slow down alone. Name one or two policies proposed to reduce the risk.
items.answer: Examples: a US-China dialogue and incident channel; using that dialogue to develop shared guidelines for rapid capability growth and prepare verification (IFP); agreed international red lines; a compute-capped treaty verified by chip tracking; funding verification R&D and a frontier-state incident hotline.
keys: US-China dialogue and incident channel
Joint guidelines and verification prep via bilateral dialogue (IFP Rec. 22)
International red lines (e.g., no AI in nuclear launch)
Compute-capped treaty with chip-tracking verification
Verification R&D funding and incident hotline
items.x: Supporters argue unilateral restraint fails if rivals keep racing, and verification makes cheating detectable enough that compliance pays. The White House said in September 2026 that the US and China agreed to an AI incident channel; Beijing did not immediately confirm. Skeptics such as Chris McGuire (CFR) call a US-China deal on AI development very unlikely, and CNAS authors note verification tools are immature.

items.p: IFP's report on automated AI R&D recommends tightening chip and chipmaking-equipment export controls. According to IFP, what is the purpose of extending the US AI lead in this context?
items.answer: To give the US more time and more leverage to manage the risks of AI R&D automation, for example time for resilience work and leverage in international talks.
keys: More time to manage automated AI R&D risks
More leverage, including in international negotiations
items.x: IFP is the Institute for Progress. The section is titled 'Extend the US AI lead to give the US more time and leverage to manage AI R&D automation risks'. Other supporters of chip controls make a similar argument: a lead could be spent on safety work or used as leverage for an international agreement.

items.p: Suppose Congress considers overriding state frontier AI laws such as California's SB 53. Name one or two preemption designs that have been proposed, and the main concern opponents raise.
items.answer: Examples: a blanket moratorium on state AI laws; preemption traded for binding federal frontier duties; a federal floor that lets states go further. Opponents' concern: states are currently the only governments regulating frontier AI, so preemption without a strong federal floor removes the only binding rules.
keys: Blanket moratorium (stripped from a 2025 bill by a 99-1 Senate vote)
Preemption traded for a federal frontier standard (FRONTIER Act)
Federal floor where states may go further
Opponents: removes the only binding rules absent a strong federal floor
items.x: Supporters of preemption, such as Dean Ball and Alan Rozenshtein, argue one national standard avoids a burdensome patchwork and frontier risk is national in scope. Executive Order 14365 (Dec. 2025) directs a Justice Department task force to challenge state laws; Democrats' GUARDRAILS Act would nullify it. As of mid-October 2026 no federal statute preempts state AI law.

items.p: Suppose a few firms control chips, cloud computing and frontier models together, and government comes to depend on them. Name one or two policies proposed to spread control.
items.answer: Examples: merger-style review of lab and cloud-provider partnerships; structural separation of chips, cloud and models; nondiscrimination rules for cloud access; requiring government to buy from multiple AI vendors; public compute and public AI options such as NAIRR.
keys: Review of lab-hyperscaler partnerships as mergers
Structural separation of the AI stack
Cloud nondiscrimination or utility rules
Multi-vendor government procurement
Public compute (e.g., NAIRR)
items.x: NAIRR is the National AI Research Resource. The FTC studied the Microsoft-OpenAI, Amazon-Anthropic and Google-Anthropic partnerships under its Section 6(b) authority. On the other side, FTC Commissioner Melissa Holyoak described massive competition among foundation-model developers (2025 speech).
